AN APRIL SONG. My heart leaps up on a bright Sprirag day, When I look out to the sky, And see the clouds in light dis,,Lay Floating gently by. So was it, when I was a Now, though my hairs are gray, My heart throbs witifi the self-same joy On a shining P,pril day: nine, shine, 0 April bright, And drive dull care away! Youtl:..es the season made for joys," old song thus doth say, "ALI can make a merry noise, Although my hairs are gray. There's danger in youth's wild delights And hotly spurred desires; But safety dwells with sober sprights, And chastely glowing fires. Shine, shine, 0 April bright, And drive dull care away! If thou wouldst earn a poet's thanks On a shining April day, Oh, take me where the primrose pranks The gently sloping brae, Where its sweet song the bvnie purls Beneath the birchen spray, And the fresh-sprouting leaf uncurls Its greenness to the day. Shine, shine, 0 April bright, And drive dull care away! And let me hear the mavis pour, His rich full-throated lay, Unbosoming his redundant store Of gladness to the day; And let me ban all moody thoughts To Limbo far away, When all the air is quick with notes Of happy life to-day. Shine, shine, 0 April bright, And drive dull care away ! And let no breath invade my ear Of crude unreasoned babble, And let no fretful word come near Of Whig and Tory squabble! And while on Pentland's grassy swell I weave my song with.glee, Lit war with wrangling factions dwell; God's peace abides with me. Shine, shine, 0 April bright, And drive dull care away! Right lovely is thy world, 0 God, And I will praise it ever, While I look up from earth's green sod To Thee, the General GIVER! Thy grace did rein my youthful will, All strength to Thee belongs, And Thou, when hairs are gray, Lost fill The old man's breast with songs. Shine, shine, 0 April bright, And drive dull care away! Joinz STUART MACKIE.

Losses by 'Fire: Money spent for cigars. How many ladies go to church to gaze upon each other's -sealskin sacques ? This is really sacquereligions. There is but one road to lead us to God—humility; all other ways would only lead astray, even were they fenced in with all virtues.—L' Abbe Boileau.

- A little fellow in a primary school was asked by his leacher to spell the word knife. After he had correctly ,4lone so, he added, "But what's the K for ?" A little boy being asked if Ihe was dux of his class, re- plied, "I am where the head of the class used to be, but the teacher has turned the class round." _ _ _

"How far is it to Manyunk ?" asked a weary Irishman, who was going there afoot. "Seven miles," was the reply. "Whom do you wish to see there?" "Faith it's myself I'd loik to see-there 1" was the retort.

A little boy complained of his bedfellow taking half his bed. "Why not ?" replied his mother; "he is entitled to the half, is he not ?" "Yes, mother; but would you like him to take all the soft for his half? He insists on sleep- ing in the middle of the bed, and I am obliged to sleep on both sides of him." "How Do You LIKE Your?. NEIGHBOUR ?"—The com- pany must seat themselves round the room, leaving plenty of space in the middle for passing to and fro. One person left standing then begins the game by putting the question, "How do you like your neighbour ?" lo anyone he pleases. The answer must be either "Not at all," or "Very much." Should the reply be "Not at all," the lady or gentleman is requested to say what other two members of the company would be preferred instead as neighbours, when the new neigh- hours and the old must immediately change places. During *e transition the questioner may endeavour to secure a seat I forhimself, leaving out one of the four who have been strug- gling for seats to take the place of the questioner. When the reply "Very much" i given, everyone in the room must change places. The questioner, therefore will easily find a seat for himself, and the person left standing must take his place as interrogator.—Cassell's Book of Sports and Pas- tintos, for Apra. . DRAWINGS.—Gustave Dore, the designer and illus- trator, is certainly a person of quite extraordinary parts. His most individual work 'has the gigantic vagueness, the rapidity, the impossible and affecting unreality of a super- natural dream. He thought in pictures; and his thoughts are those of one to whom the unseen, intangible world is more friendly and more fruitful than the world in which men dwell. They take no heed of flesh wad blood, nor the essentials of life, nor the unalterable truths of nature. They deal with an actuality of their own projecting and con- triving; with a universe of figments and appearances with a scheme of things that is no more than a scheme of shadows. They work and move in a region of dimness and illusion, of shifting shapes and processions of strangeness—a region remote from fact, and peopled with impossibilities alone. Enchanted castles; landscapes from the borderland of cre- ation ; frenzies of architecture; turrets that topple up to heaven and abysms dbven „hell deep; forests grim with mystery and presences of magic ; rocks that seem possessed by an evil spirit; parades of monsters and chimeras ; a phan- tasmagoria of violence and terror and wonderment—this is the general impression of Dore's mind and Dore's art.—The Magazine of Art for April.

CHILDREN'S WONDERFUL WORDS. Keep a guard on your words, my darlings, For words are weGjerful things; They are sweet like the bees' fresh honey, Like the bees they have terrible stings. They can bless like the cheering sunshine, And brighten a lonely life ; They can cut in the strife of anger Like an open, two-edged knife. Let them pass through your lips unchallenged If their errand is true and kind; If they come to support the weary To comfort and help the blind. If a bitter, revengeful spirit Prompts the words, let them be unsaid; They may flash through the brain like lightning. Or fall on the heart like lead. Keep them back if they're cold and. cruel, Under bar, and lock, and seal; The wounds they make my darlings, Are always slow to heal. May peace guard our lives, and ever, From this time of your early youth, May the words that you daily utter Be the beautiful words of truth.

A SOUTH AFRICAN SUPERSTITION.—The people seem to ,have retained little or no knowledge of a supreme being, responsibility, or a future state. One tradition they had. The Moon once sent a message with the hare to mankind, to say that as she (the moon) died and lived again so after death man would live again. The hare came and told them, "After death you will live no more." On returning, the Moon asked, "Well, what sort'of a message have you taken So mankind ?" "I have told them," said the hare, "that after death they will live no more." "Then," said the *Moon, flying into a great passion, "why have you taken each a false message to mankind ?" and, snatching up a &Whet that was at hand, she fetched the hare such a blow ea the upper lip as oleft it in two; and that's the reason whyrwhen you see a hare, it has a cloven lip. The hare, in return, flew into the face of the Moon, and scratched it se violently that that's the reason why you see all those dark marks on the face of the full moon. Whenever they saw a hare, they said, "See, there goes a hare; if it had brought a right message, then after death we should have lived. again; but it brought us a wrong message, and new after death we shall live no more." For this reason they alwaYa regarded the hare as an accursed thing, and never ate its flesTa whilst they continued heathens. Such was the account given to Mr. Ridedale by David Afrikaner.— " Scenes (IQ Achentures in Great Namaqualand," by .the Rev. Benjamin Rictsdale.

THE LEGEND O' Tii; HOLY THORN.—To the south of the. little town of Glastonbury rises, as has been already .said, one of those steep ridgy hills 80 characteristic of this Part of Somersetshire. To the eastern part the name of the Tor" is given; the long "hog's back" to the west " bears the singular title of Weary-all-Hill. This is accounted for as follows :--St. Joseph and his followers had wandered far, and, as the 4Avlight was fading on a Christmas Eve, piled up the slopes of this hill. As they reached the top, and the island oasis of Avallon lay before them, the old man, "weary-all" with the journey, halted for rest, and throat his thornwood staff into the ground. For awhile the little .company reposed; then St. Joseph rose, and stretched out his hand to take up his staff 'and resume his journey. But lo! a miracle: the dry wood had been quickened into life; it had struck roots into the ground, and put forth green leaves which were soon followed by white blossoms. It was the sign to them, like the locust alighting on the robe of Gregory, that here their wanderings were to end. So They descended the slope, and took up their abode, as we have told, on the more level ground at its foot. But, so long as Glastonbury Abbey flourished, so long did this thorn-tree, or one of its descendants, continue to put forth leaves and duly blossom at the Christmas-tide. Speci- mens are still living which, undoubtedly, do not unfre- quently exhibit an abnormal habit of winter buddlitg, though net with such regularity as was claimed for it by.its medieval guardians. Glastonbury also boasted of aro iracu- leas walnut-tree, which did not put forth its leaves till St Bartiabk Day (June 11th),-' Our Own Chuntry" for April.

A cow, the property of Mr. Cleveland, of Walberswick, Suffolk, has just produced twins, making twelves calves in eight Years. The Prince of Wales has intimated his intention of visit- ing the show of the Royal Agricultural Society to be held in York next July. At the show of the Highland and Agricultural Society in Inverness this year it is stated that the directors have re- solved to introduce the system of having the show managed by stewards for the different departments, instead of, as hitherto, leaving the whole of the work of supervision to be undertaken by the secretary. 4. HORSE CORONER'S REPORT.—At the meeting of the Islington Vestry on Tuesday, Mr. Caleb J. Hunt, inspector of houses for slaughtering horses, reported that- during the past 12 months the animals brought to the slaughterhouses ' in his district have been as follows :—Horses alive, 4,170; cows, dead, 5,650; bulls, dead, 20; heifers, dead, 6; mules, dead, 6; donkeys, alive, 14; donkeys, dead, 20; stirks, dead, 2. He also stated that he had been the means of re- storing to their owners two live horses. PROFESSOR TANNER, of the Institute of Agriculture, South Kensington, lecturing in Shropshire on the economi- cal production of meat, spoke of the inevitable waste of food, and compared the process of feeding to the stoking of a steam engine. A great deal of fuel is necessarily wasted without actually contributing to the work performed by the machine. It is "burned to waste," goes up the chimney in the form of smoke or of lost heat, while a certain quan- tity is required merely to keep the engine in motion. In the feeding of animals as much as one-third of the food is sometimes wasted. And the longer the process is about, the greater is the amount of waste which is thus incurred. Some of it must be wasted;but that which is expended when animals are fed without making progress, is wasted wholly. THE RAVAGES OF RODENTS.-. 111 Arizona and California, and also in Western Texas and New Mexico, the farmers have annually to contend against the destructive habits of certain rodents, whose ravages have often devastated entire sections. The centfal and southern portions of California especially are overrun by innumerable squirrels, which in- crease with such rapidity that the means hitherto employed to destroy them have proved wholly inadequate. In Ari- zona, New Mexico and Western Texas, several varieties of rabbits are equally destructive with the squirrels of Cali- fornia, and the huge field rats of Southern Arizona and the frontier. These destructive animals eat the tender shoots of the cereals as soon as they appear above ground; but. worse than all they burrow in the earth to such an extent that in a few, hours a vast field of thriving grain will pre- sent the appearance of a thoroughly ploughed plain. A sys- tematic war of extermination has become necessary. THE Sccrrrtsit FARMERS' ALLIANCE.—At a largely at- tended meeting of farmers held on Tuesday in Dundee it was resolved to form branches of the Scottish Farmers' Alliance in Forfarshire and, Fifeshire. Mr. J. W. Barclay-, M.P. for Forfar-hire, was one of the speakers at the meet- ing. The principal resolution was as follows :—" That this meeting views with satisfaction the proposal of the Govern- ment to introduce this session a measure giving tenants legal compensation for their improvements in and on the soil, and expresses the hope that the basis on which such compensation will be calculated will be the increased letting value of the holding due to these improvements, such measure to be made applicable to existing leases." Another resolution was to the effect That the interpretatiodby the Court of Session of the provision relating to trapping, in the Ground Game Act goes very far to nulify the benefits hoped for from that Act, and places farmers who had the right to kill game before the passing of the Act in a much worse position, and ought forthwith to be abolished." All the resolutions were carried unanimously.
DEEP SEA SOUNDINGS.—It is stated that the distinction

of making the deepest sounding in the Atlantic ever yet re- corded has been achieved by the officers of the Coast and Geodelic Survey steamer Blake, recently returned to New York from a two months' survey. The deepest sounding ever before reported was 3,862 fathoms, which was made by the Challenger, sent out by the Royal Society. The depth reached by the Blake was 4,561 fathoms. The place of sounding was 75 miles north of San Juan, Porto Rico, andnot far from the point at which the Challenger sank her deepest lead. THE CONCENTRATION OF SOLAR HEAT.—M. Delaurier describes in Les Mondes a new system of concentration of solar heat. The principle is that if the air be heated in a closed space, the hottest layers rise to the upper parts, and in this region the temperature will rise more and more if the calorific action be prolonged, and suitable precautions be taken against cooling. Thus, if the inclosure have the form of a pyramid or a eone, an apparatus, both curious and variously useful, may be had at little cost. M. Delau- rier uses a double envelope of glass witk a layer of air in the interval. On the shaded side the outer envelope is covered with light wooden shutters coated with bright metal. This arrangement is especially useful for winter or a cold climate. At the centre of the apparatus, on a wooden base, ire fixed vertical radiating partitions of copper blackened by oxidation, and on the edges of these are cemented the trapezoidal plates of glass, which form the first envelope. The apparatus is not hermetically closed below. M. Delaurier considers that it would, besides being industrially useful, make an excellent pyrrheliometer. REMARKABLE ELECTRICAL DISCOVERY.— THE TRANS- MISSION OF SlGHT.—Applications of electricity are not only making rapid progress in every part of Europe, but also in the southern hemisphere. There come, indeed, from Otago, New Zealand, details of an invention as marvellous as any yet recorded in the annals of electrical science. The Rev. Mr. Gilbert, of Christchurch, in a recent address, told his audience that it was now proved to be possible to con- vey, by means of electricity, vibrations of light—not only to speak with your distant friend, but actually to see him. The electroscope—the name of the instrument which enabled ; to do this—was the very latest scientific discovery, and to Dr. Guidrah, of Victoria, belonged the proud distinction of being its inventor and perfecter. Mr. Gilbert stated that a trial of this wonderful instrument had taken place at Mel- bourne, in the presence of some 40 scientific and public men, and that it had been a great success. Sitting in a dark room, they saw projected on a large disc of white burnished i metal the racecourse at Flemington, with its myriad of lactive beings. Minute details stood out with perfect fidelity to the original, and as they looked at the wonderful picture j through binocular glasses, it was difficult to imagine that they were not actually on the course itself, and moving among those whose actions they could so completely scan. —Times. COMPARATIVE STRENGTH OF MEN AND WO3IEN.—From Paris we receive the report of experiments conducted with an instrument on which the palm of the hand is placed, and 11, downward pressure exercised. Sixty-four men, aged from I 25 to 45 years, belonging to the middle classes, and whose ordinary occupation did not necessitate any sort of manual work, were prevailed upon to try their strength. The ; strongest man was able to produce a pressure equivalent to , 85 kilogrammes, the weakest to 40 kilogrammes; and the average was 56 kilogrammes. There was also- an average difference of 10 kilogrammes between the strength of the right and left hand; but the shorter men were nearly as ; strong as the tall men, as an average difference of only three kilogrammes was noted. The number of women whose I services were secured for exactly the same trial of strength was unfortunately not the same. There were only 52 women, but these were taken from the same class of society. ; The force of the strongest woman amounted only to 44 I kilogrammes, and that of the weakest to 16 kilogrammes; _ _

After the clergyman had united a happy pair not long ago an awful silence ensued, which was broken by an im- patient youth exclaiming, "Don't be so unspeakably happy !" THE ROLL OF WEDDINGS.—At the end of the first year comes the cotton wedding. At two years comes the paper. At three the leather. At the close of five comes die wooden. At the seventh anniversary the friends assemble at the woollen. At ten comes the tin. At twelve years the silken and line linen. At fifteen the crystal wedding. At twenty the friends gather with the china. At twenty-five the married couple who have been true to their vows for a quar- ter of a century are rewarded with, silver gifts. /Wm this ' period forward the tokens of esteem become rapidly more valuable. When the thirtieth anniversary is reached they are presented with pearls. At the fortieth come rubies. At the fiftieth occurs the golden wedding. Beyond that time the aged couple are allowed to enjoy their many gifts in peace. If, however, by any possibility they should reach their seventy-fifth anniversary they are presented with the rarist gifts to be obtained, at the celebration of their dia- mond wedding.—Leals Mercury. WRENN INTELLIGENCE.
Six persons have been killed by an explosion on board a tow-boat on the Mississippi River, near Belmont, Missouri.
Cremation is becoming very general in Japan, and at the present time the number of bodies disposed of in this way is about 9,000 each year.

'1 here is a report_ from Cape Coast Castle that the King of Ashantee bas abdicated, and that the whole country has been thrown into a state of confusion. On Wednesday the National Theatre at Berlin was de- stroyed by tire, nothing being saved but part of the wardrobe and the property rooms. The fire broke out at noon, but its oligin is not known. • Louise Michel, who led the Paris mob in the recent dis- turbance in that tfity, has been arrested in the French capi- tal on warrants charging her with the pillage of bakers' shops at the head of an armed band. From Colombo, Ceylon, we learn that serious riots have occurred between the Buddhists and the Roman Catholics in consequence of the latter objecting to a religious body who desired to parade the streets with a cross accompanied by an emblem, which they thought implied a reflection on their religion.

a. Jules Ferry, the French Premier, states that the Government has arranged to re-purchase, for £24%000, the manuscripts in the Ashharnham collection, which are said to have been stolen by Libri. M. Ferry complimented the "British Museum authorities" for the manner in which they had recognised the claims of France in this matter. HORRIBLE MURDER OF A GIRL IN FRANCR.—A terrible muider is reported from the department of Donba,in France. A girl named Herminia Aubry, fourteen years of age, has been assassinated in her home, near Pontarlici, during the absence of her parents. She was stabbed in no fewer than seven different places. Robbery is believed to have been the motive for the crime.

TERRIBLE DYNAMITE EXPLOSION : FIFTY PERSONS KILLEb AND MANit INJURED.—A: telegram from Rome dated Thursday says,—A store of dynamite temporarily estab- lished at Passo Corise, near Rome, on the railway to Flor- ence, for works which were being constructed on the line there, exploded to-day. It 's stated that fifty persons were killed and many injured. Thirteen dead bodies have already been extracted from the ruins.

THE NIHILISTS AND THE CZAR'S CORONATION. - The Nihilists have issued a proclamation in which they dis- tinctly annoum their intention, if possible, to murder the Czar on the occasion of his coronation, which is fixed for the 15th May. The would-be regicides conclude their pro- clamaton as follows :—" We will strike once more for Russia's freedom, and we call:, upon all true-minded Russians to aid us in sweeping away the mass of corruption and falsehood under which the country is at present groan- ing." The proclamation is printed in red letters and with a red border.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. It is expected that as the result of a private inquiry, at which 67 witnesses have been examined, three or four per- sons will-shortly be arrested for the murder of Mrs. Smythe in county Westmeath, a year ago. At Cork Assizes, yesterday week, a young man named Timothy O'Keefe was found guilty of murdering his uncle at King Williamstown on the 30th of April last, and was sentenced to death. He is to be hanged on the anniversary of the murder. The prieener was tried at the winter assizes, when the jury disagreed. A Cork correspondent says an apparently well-founded suspicion has been entertained that a factory has been in existence there for the manufacture of dangerous explosives. The discovery in Liverpool of two machines has confirmed that suspicion, and the action of the potice in searching the houses of suspected persons is believed to be with the object of finding some clue to the existence of this factory. A reaction against Parnellism has been observed at several important local elections in Ireland. At Athlone, Boyle, Carrick-on-Suir, and other places, gentlemen who were ex- pelled from office on boards of guardians last year were on Saturday re-elected by large majorities over Parnellite can- didates. This is important as affecting the pockets of the ratepayers, because some of the "National" Guardians have shown extraordinary liberality in voting away public money in aid of their political friends and followers. Dayerr ON DYNAmTE.--Micnael Davitt,writing from Rich- mond Prison to the chairman of the Glasgow Young Ireland Society, says :—Dynainite can only destroy public buildings, and thereby exasperate the English democracy.' Better to work patiently but perseveringly for 20 more years, if need be than to play again into our enemies' hands, and destroy all chance of social and national reform in this generation by indulging in the old impatience and giving the rein to despair and revenge. Mr. Sackville West, the British Minister at Washington, has formerly called the attention of the American Govern- ment to the utterances of the Irieh leaders in that country. 'I he Cabinet, it is stated, agreed that in the present sitnatien of affairs the American Government is not justified in in- terfering with the Irish sympathisers. The President adopted as his own the opinion of his Cabinet, and he has communicated this decision to Mr. West, with the assurance that the United States Government will use its utmost endeavours to observe both its national and international obligations. THE APPROACHING TRIALS: DISCHARGE OP AN INVIN- CIELE.—It is stated that the preparations for the trials of the prisoners charged with complicity in the Phoenix Park murders haveebeen completed. The proceedings will com- mence next week, and it is calculated that they will last for a month. Brady will first be put in the dock, and if the jury cannot agree in his case, it is said that the trials will be stopped for the time, and an application will be made on behalf of the Crown fore change of the venue from Dublin to Belfast. None of the accused, except those who are al- i ready known as informers or approvers, will be accepted as ' Queen's evidence. John Dwyer, one of the Invincibles who were committed for trial, has been discharged from Kil- mainham on the ground of ill-health. The case against him, however, was not very strong. It is expected that more startling revelations than any which have yet been made public will be elicited at the trials, including proof of the payment and receipt of money far the purposes of assassina- tion.

Accounts come from Cattara of a desperate conflict be- tween Montenegrins and Arnauts. Twenty-five of the latter who were crossing over in boats from the island of Oranjina to the mainland were attacked by 30 Montenegrins, also in 1 boats. The encounter lasted two hours. It began with the tiring of muskets at long range; but when the boats came nearer it was continued with revolvers, and at last with yata-1 ghans. The Montenegrins, who were the more numerous,' and had their yataghans with them, finally overcame the Arnauts and killed them all; nine of their own number were killed, and eleven wounded. DYNAMITE OUTRAGES.—Dynamite outrages and plots con- tinue to be reported from various parts of the Continent. One night last week a cartridge was placed under the door- way of a miner's house at Montceau-les-Mines in France, which exploded with great violence , and wrecked the lower part of the premises. The occupants, who were upstairs at the time, happily escaped uninjured. It would seem that the death of the head of the family had been threatened by the Anarchist Executive Committee. Adv.ices from St. Petersburg report an attack by the police on a rendezvous of Nihilists, which resulted in eight arrests. A forcible resist- ance was offered to the capture, and two policemen and a gendarme were injured in the struggle. Finding escape hopeless, one of the conspirators stabbed himself during the melee, and died from his wound. The gang were in posses- sion of a quantity of dynamite. MURDER IN A WINESIIOP.—A savage murder has been committed. just in the rear of the Madeleine, in Paris. It' was immediately followed by the suicide of the murderer. The victim is Marie Louisa Vinsonneau, a young married woman, and the mother of two children. She And her hus- band kept a wineshop in the street mentioned. In the absence of the husband, an acquaintance of both husband and wife, named Andre Baronnat, entered the shop in a state of intoxication. Madame Vinsonneau was sitting behind the counter with her little girl, achild of fouryears. Accord- ing to the account of the little girl, Baronnat asked for a glass of absinthe, which was refuied. Baronnat imme- diately drew a revolver from his pocket and fired twice upon Madame Vinsonneau. She fell bleeding on the floor, and subsequently died. The report Of the pistol brought the neighbours to the shop, when the murderer, apparently sobered by the sight of his work, fired his weapon into his mouth, killing himself on the spot. Baronnatt, a man of 28, was a coachman, formerly in the service of the Duc.de Noailles.

RUSSIAN PREPARATIONS TO OCCUPY ARMENIA.—The special correspondent of the' Daily News, writing from Trebizond under date March 18, describes a 'great concen- tration of Russian troops and war materials at and about Tiflis, and says that Trebizond is full'of revived rumours that Russia is preparing for an occupation of Armenia, and that the Armenians would welcome the protection of the Czar. The Daily News, commenting upon this news, which it regards as authentic, says : By the Berlin Treaty Turkey undertook to protect the Armenians and to give them reforms, but she entered into a compact with the signatory Powers, not with us alone. And the wild protectorate which the late Cabinet by the Anglo-Turkish Convention pledged itself to establish over Turkey in Asia was so impossible in itself that probably it has long been forgotten by most of our readers It was to take effect only if the Ottoman Government carried out the necessary reforms throughout Asia, and the Ottoman Government, in spite of all the pressure put upon it by Lord Salisbury, obstinately refused to carry out a single reform. We are in no way bound then to defend Turkish rule in Armenia, even if desired. It is clear that, great as is the might of the British Empire, it is not mighty enough to maintain the Ottoman Empire much longer. The Ottoman Empire is rapidly dying. The Sultan refuses to carry out apy reform, to make even any material change in his system of government, and disorder, anarchy, and dis- affection are rife in every one of his provinces. If, then, we were to resist the Russians and drive them out of Armenia, we could maintain the Turkish Empire only by occupying and practically governing it ourselves. But to add to all our other responsibilities that of governing the Turkish Empire is what we apprehend few sane men at this time of day will advocate. TERRIBLE BOILER EXPLOSION IN FRANCE: 31 PERSONS KILLED AND 65 INJURED.—A disastrous accident occurred on Satuulay in one of the factories of the Compagniedes Forges de Caropagne, at Marnaval, near St. Dizier. A vertical boiler exploded a few minutes past eight, when all the hands, having finished their first breakfast, had returned to work. The force of the explosion was terrific the upper part of the boiler being blown through the roof of the work- shop, and the bricks and masonry surrounding the boiler projected with such force against the•walls that the remain- ing portion of the roof fell in, killiag or wounding most of those who had been left unhurt by the original explosion. The scene oPconsternation which followed was heartrending.l Women and children rushed to the spot searching for fathers, brothers, or friends among the heap of ruins. The director of the foundry, whose offices are at St. Dizier, at once organised assistance, and with the authorities, the firemen, and the police, hastened to the scene of the catastrophe. In a short time the foundry was surrounded by an immense crowd. The firemen acted most courageously, and were indefatigable in their sad work of extricating the dead and wounded from beneath the ruins. The cries of the wounded, some of whom are horribly mutilated, were terrible. Thirty-one persons were killed on the spot, and of the 65 wounded, who were transported by an irony of fate in the wagons of a travelling circus to the Hospital of St. Dizier, about 20 are so seriously injured that they are not expected to survive. The cause of the explosion is not yet known with any degree of certainty. It is supposed that by negligeece the water in the boiler had been allowed to run low. The chief puddler, who was working at a furnace close to the boiler, escaped miracu- lously, with only a few insignificant scratches on his hands; but curiously enough he cannot say how he reached the banks of the river Marne, where he found himself a few seconds after the explosion. Two men working by his side were killed, and his two sons, who were occupied in the foundry, are also among the dead. A subscription in aid of the victims had been opened.

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. -- TUESDAY.—Before Mr. J. M. Yates, judge. ACTION AGAINST A WIDNES ENGINEER.—J. J. Steward, autioneer, Chester, sued Win. Crabtree, engineer, Mersey- street, Widnes, for the sum of £5 10s., the value of goods sold to the plaintiff at a sale in September.—Mr. Hitchen appeared for the plaintiff.—Mr. Steward said the defendant attended a three days' sale which ha held at Newton Hall, and there purchased several things for which he ought 0 have at one paid. He, however, did not do so, and the things were left on the premises for a few days, when the defendant called, and was allowed to remove them, with the exception of one or two, which were lying there. He had not paid for them.—The defendant said. the delivery of the whole of the goods was refused to him, but His Honour said the moment the goods were knocked down the debt was in- curred, and gave a verdict for the plaintiff. He told the defendant that if the goods were not delivered to him he could sue the plaintiff for undue detention. 'A HORSE IN A LI3IE PIT: CLAIM FOR DAMAGES.— Richard Forshaw, boatman, Shaw-street. Runcorn, brought an action against James Weir and John Acton, to recover £l4 damages for the loss of his hot se.—The plaintiff was represented by Mr. Taylor, barrister-at-law, Liverpool (instructed by Mr. Burton) ; and Mr. Fletcher, of North- wich, appeared for the defendants.—A jury was empannelled to hear the case.—Mr. Taylor stated that since the action was entered Weir, one of the oo - defendants, had since died by misfortune of some kind—by acci- dentally shooting himself—but in order to explain Mr. Acton's liability, it would be necessary for him to deal with the circumstances under which they alleged that Weir was himself liable. Forshaw was a canal boatman, and the horse in question was the one which towed his boat along the canal. Ile made an arrangement with Mr. Weir by which he should for a certain sum stable his horse at his farm, and on the night of the 10th January the horse was put up there. Next morning about four o'clock, when it was dark, Forshaw was taking the horse from the stable to the canal side along a road which had been used by various people for over 30 years in journeying from Weir's farm to , the canal. As he was proceeding along, the horse became excited and slipped into a lime pit, which was five feet deep, and contained lime to the depth of two feet six. In spite of all the efforts of the plaintiff, and people who he called to his aid, the hairs on its body were all singed off, its eyes ' were burned out, and after it was got out it possessed •a mere , remnant of life, and soon ceasel to exist. This was a serious loss to Mr. Forshaw, and the question before the jury was who was reanonsible. The case originally against Weir was , that this pit was dangerous, having a steep incline to it and no protection around it, and that it was his duty to fence it ' for the protection of the public. Mr. Acton was a contrac- tor, and was employed at the time in question either by Mr. Weir or the landlord to, make certain alterations to the farm buildings, and he dug the pit for the purpose of making lime. Of course using the pit for that purpose it was Mr. Acton's duty to have fenced it in order to prevent persons travelling along the road from falling i nto the pit. The question was whether Mr. Acton left the pit in a negligent and defenceless condition, and if in the opinion of the jury that was so, he asked for a verdict for the plaintiff. He called the plaintiff, who con- firmed counsel's statement, but stated that since the time of the accident a bank about two feet high was made round the pit. He had travelled the road for the hat 50 years, but had never noticed the pit until the morning he got in with his horse. The horse was worth £l4 —By Mr. Fletcher : The horse belonged to Edwin Tuckey, from whom he had it on trial. He was taking the actiore for Tuckey.—Ricbard Burroughs, foreman joiner, of 8, Vine-street, Runcorn, proved the plan of the land where the accident took place.— Wm. Morris, captain of the flat Gertie, described the efforts made to rescue the horse from its position, and deposed that he had travelled the road for over 30 years."—Edwin Tuckey valued the horse at £l4.—Mr. C. L. Evans, agent to Sir Richard Brooke' said he engaged Mr. Acton, the defen- dant, to repair the farm buildings. He believed that Mr. Acton had used the pit for the purpose of the repairs, and he had told him (witness) that he had always considered , himself the owner of the lime.—By Mr. 'Fletcher: Mr. Acton finished the werk in November last year.—George Pennington, farmer, Norton, said he was formerly a builder, and in 1879, whilst repairing Weir's house, he dug a lime pit in exactly the same spot as the one referred to. But, as it was his duty to do, he filled it up with cinders when he had finished. The road which went past was for the convenience of Mr. Weir.—This closed the case for the plaintiff, and Mr. Flet- cher submitted that there was no negligence made out against Acton.—His Honour: There is no evidence that Acton made the pit to go to the jury.—Mr. Taylor: There is evidence that he used the pit.—His Honour: There is no evidence to go to the jury that the accident was caused by the lime pit being there, but by the horse taking fright at something else.—Mr. Taylor made certain statements, of which he asked his Honour to take a note. His Honour complied, and entered a nonsuit against the plaintiff on the ground that he was of opinion that Acton did not make the bole; that there was no evidence of negligence on his part, or that the accident was caused by his negligence. He gave leave to enter a fresh action.

If mutton is better than veni- son, why does venison cost so much more?" "Vy?" re- plied the capitalist. "1 vill tell you vy. In dish world de people alvash prefer what is deer to vat ish sheep. THE END OF A FOUR YEARS' VOYAGE.-At the Liverpool City Police court, on Tuesday, tefore Mr. Raffles, stipen- diary magistrates three young women, named Mary Ann Lomons, Alice Flannigan, and Mary Ann Lester, were charged on suspicion with having on the previous evening stolen £4 from a coloured seaman named Joseph Mellor. From the evidence it appeared that prosecutor got drunk, and having met the three prisoners took them to the Royal Court Theatre. Police-constable 808 (Flood), who was in plain clothing, afterwards saw the prisoners around the man, and took them in custody on suspicion of stealing. On the prisoner Flannigan being searched £2 10s. in gold and a few shillings were found upon her, which she alleged was given her by prosecutor to keep. Very little money was found upon the other women. Prosecutor said that he might have given the money to mind, but he could not tell what had become of £4. Altogether be had about £24 upon him in notes and gold.—Mr. Raffles: That is a veiy roose way to carry money about. Where did you get it from ? Prosecutor : I was paid off last Saturday after a four years' voyage and came from San Francisco.—Mr. Raffles: How much did you receive ?—Prosecntor : £194. I kept £42 myself and sent £l5O to my wife, who is in Perth, Scotland, and lam going there to-day. As no case could be made out against the prisoners they were discharged.

div.head: HOUSEHOLD PETS.
div.p: HOUSEHOLD PETS.

PIGEONS.—THE FRILLED VARIETIES.—One of the most beautiful of all the sections of pigeons is that known by the name of Frills, which name includes the owls, the turbits, the satinettes, and their many sub-varieties. All these are more or less related, and have come from eastern lands. There are large numbers of those known as Eastern frilled toys imported from Asia Minor and from North Africa. Some of the very best foreign owls came from the latter continent, and are unique specimens. Owls derive their name from the beak, which is short and stoat, turned down, and with the upper mandible curving down over the lower, in as even a. curve as possible with the whole profile of the head. The head itself is desired as globular as possible, with the eye standing out well, and the beak wattle as even, convex, and fairly developed as possible. Below the beak or chin is what is known as the "gullet," which is a development of loose skin like a dewlap. And below this is the frill running down on to the breast, The carriage of a good owl should be up- right, with the head thrown back, the feather short, the chest broad, and the feathers rounded. In colour blues, silvers, whites, and blacks are common, with admixtures of 1 the same. Turbits resemble owls in many points, but the head is longer, the gape of the mouth far wider, and the beak is not so short, nor yet so down faced, but it is similar as to beak wattle gullet, and frill; the last-named point is, however, preferred larger than in the owl. The chief dis- tinction is the peak or crest, which should be as high and pointed as possible, with the feathers meeting evenly, so as to form an even ridge or mane behind, coping down to the back of the neck. The turbit is decidedly small, but longer in feather than the owl. The colour of this variety is a white body, except the shoulders of the wings, which are found black, blue, blue-chequered, silver, red, yellow, and dun, and the whole appearance of a good coloured bird is very striking. It is impossible to attempt to describe the many other varieties of these toys, but the whole of them are characterised by very great beauty. Some of them are clean and others feather-legged, and all are regarded as high class birds. Turbiteens are vety like turbits, but have a coloured spot on the forehead, and a cheek-mark at each side of the head. Satinettes are more like owls, and are feather- legged, but the colour on the body and wings is laced. Brunettes are simply lighter coloured satinettes, whilst Bluettes and Silverettes are so named to denote their special 1 colours. Blondinettes are coloured all over, and blue vizors and dominoes have been produced by crossing the Eastern varieties with some other breeds. SNAKES.—The cage described by us is large enough for small reptiles, but without large and well-built ones none of the bigger varieties of snakes may be kept. There are many gentlemen and ladies who keep young snakes of the larger kinds, but they can only do this for a time, for when they begin to approach maturity they have to be disposed of. Some of those that now are to be seen in the London Zoological Gardens have been presented in this way. No one can realise without witnessing it, the enormous strength of large snakes, and without proper places to keep, them in they would be actually dangerous inmates of a house. This is true respecting the non-poisonous varieties, and there- fore, whilst speaking of snakes as pets, we must give this warning to show how they are to be provided for. Perhaps the most interesting of all matters in connection with snakes is to watch their incubation and growth during the earlier stages of their existence. This may be done by fitting up an ordinary fish globe or vase for the purpose. It must be filled with fine gravel or coarse sand up to the level of its largest diameter, and be furnished with a small saucer or pot, buried to the rim, for water, and a miniature tree. Over the top a piece of muslin or stout gauze is passed. This • globe must rest upon a cylindrical hot-water tin holding about four gallons, and concave at the upper end, so that the globe can sink into it to the level of the surface of the gravel. A thin piece of flannel should interpose between the glass and the metal, and the tin, which will require to be refilled with hot-water every thirty-six hours, should be enveloped with felt. CAGE BIRDS.—PARASITES.—Cage bird keepers are often troubled with parasites in their cages. If this be so, all the cracks, perches, and other likely resorts should be washed with benzoline both inside and outside the cage. !his is best done by pouring some out into a small pot, and taking a new small paint brush to put- it on. The cages must be allowed to stand a day or two in the open air, and then for the inside a strong solution of alum and cold water mixed with the whitening, and some starch or a little lump tallow should be put on rather thickly and with a clean brush, after which it should be allowed to stand a few days. After this, it is a good plan to do the outside over again with a strong solution of alum, except the cages are mahogany, when linseed will do as well. Another good thing when the biras are sitting is to puff a little Persian or Dalmatian insect powder into the nest. Well-made cats dqnot har- bour fleas, esc., but badly fitting ones, with loose wires, give every facility for these insects. RABBITS.—REARING THE YOUNG.—It is always a good plan to let the mother get her own food away fr6m the young ones. This can be done by shutting the little door between the two compartments, and she can thus get her food without being worried. It is especially important to avoid handling the young rabbits as much as possible, but they may be carefully lifted out and allowed a run about the floor when the doe is getting her food, which will have the effect of strengthening their limbs and improving their constitutions. At about three weeks old the young rabbits pass through a moult, and another when about twice that age. During both periods it is most important to take great care of them as they are very liable to a disease at that time not' unlike measles. This is the reason why many breeders prefer td keep the young ones suckling until they are about eight weeks old, so that they may have got over this difficult period. When removing these from the doe, they should not be all taken away at once, as in that case she will suffer .a great deal. Take one away at a time, and place it in a warm hutch with some other young rabbits. This is very important, as otherwise the poor little thing will suffer from cold. The next day another may be taken, and so on. Meanwhile the doe should have less succulent food, with a little salt and flowers of sulphur in the corn to dry up any milk that may be left and clear the system from impurities. It should have good food so as to keep up its strength and prepare it for the next brood. The young rab- bits will require to be kept in roomy hutches, well venti- lated, but must not be crowded. For this purpose, it is a good plan in building a stack of hutches to make the parti- tions movable, so that several can be thrown into one, and the youngsters will enjoy racing through these. They must be fed well and have a good supply of corn, with a judicious addition of roots and green stuff. The latter should not be given too freely, and plenty of hay should be served out daily. This liberal system 01 feeding will be amply repaid in the stamina and size which the animals will exhibit when grown. This is the system to be observed and con- tinued until they reach maturity, but it swill be necessary to separate the bucks from the does when they are fourteen weeks old, or earlier if it is seen to be necessary. Nork.—With the present week the series of Household Pets will cease.

div.head: PUGNACIOUS PRISONER AT RUNCORN. – .
div.p: A PUGNACIOUS PRISONER AT RUNCORN. - .

On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Edward Holland, a strong-looking fellow,,,vas charged with wandering abroad in Devonshire Place, begging alms, and also with assaulting Inspector Hollingworth. It appeared that about 6 o'clock on Saturday evening the prisoner entered the vaults of the Duke of Devonshire publichonse, and asked each person in the vaults if he could " spare a copper." Each reply was in the negative, and the prisoner became very abusive, call- ing one man a liar, and the rest of the company ignorant. He then left-the place, cursing wildly. About ten o'clock I the sam3 night he entered the bar parlour of the same house, but was ejected. When in the street, he divested himself of his coat, which he threw on the ground, and uttered a general challenge to fight. Inspector Hollingworth, who was on duty in Devonshire Place, now came upon the scene, and having been informed of the prisoner's misdeeds ordered him to clear out. The prisoner who was in drink, struck the Inspector on the nose with such violence that blood flowed, and in self defence, the Inspector used his stick upon the prisoner.—The prisoner: Is that a lie ?—The Inspector:No. He added that he was eventually compelled to look the prisoner up. He informed the pri- soner that he was an officer before the latter struck him.— Mr. C. Reynold's (to prisoner): Do you know that you are subject to a penalty for swearing.—The prisoner : It is enough to make anybody when you hear them telling lies.—Prisoner denied that he was begging, alleging that he simply inquired the way to the bridge.—Superin- tendent Williamson said men of the prisoner's class were an intolerable nuisance in Runcorn and neighbourhood. They prowled about the suburbs of the town, and compelled people to give them money. When they met with females their conduct was outrageous. One beggar actually kicked a gentleman's door because he refused to give him alms.— The prisoner: There's no fear of me doing that.—Mr. Reynolds (to prisoner) : Your behaviour in court has been so bad, and your language so bad—l never heard anybody use such language in court before—that we cannot possibly believe in your good behaviour. We believe both charges are proved, and for begging you will be imprisoned for 14 days, with hard labour; and for the assault on the officer, a month's imprisonment, with hard labour.—The prisoner: 0! (Laughter.)

Be cheerful. It is better to live in sunshine than in gloom. If a cloud rests upon your heart, turn its silver lining to your friends, and the glow of cheer it will cast upon them will be reflected on you, and the cloud will give way before the brightness and joy its own light has begotten. The climate of Austin has a wonderfully invigorating ef- fect on the intellects of young children. "How many ends has a stick of candy got ?" asked Billy Smartboy of his father. "Two, of course." "That's where you are mis- taken. I have bitten three or four ends off this stick of candy, and there are two left yet." "I don't believe you have the water of the right tem- perature. You must get a thermometer," said an Austin mother to the new coloured nurse. "What am dat ?" "It is an instrument by which you can tell if the water is too hot or too cold." I kin tell dat ar without any instru- ment. Ef de chile turns blue, den de water am too cold; and ef hit turns red, den I know dat de water am too hot." A grocer grossly insulted Mrs. Mose Schaumberg, the other day without intending it. She is an immensely stout woman, and, stepping upon the scales, playfully requested the grocer to weigh her. As he adjusted the weights, he remarked that she weighed one hundred and ninety pounds, which proved to be her exact weight. "How did you come i to guess it ?" she asked. "I am use.l to guessing at weights. ; I weighed hogs for five years in Cincinnatti."

LANCASHIRE ASSOCIATION CHALLENGE CUP FINAL TIE: BLACKBURN ROVERS V. DARWEN.—For the second time these übs met on Faturday in the final tie of the above competi- tion, and 12,000 spectators assembled to witness the match. On the first occasion, in 1880, Darwen won the game by three goals to none, and became first holders of the cup. The Black- burn Rovers, who bad held the cup fur twelve months, won on Saturday by three gonl,* to two, and carried off the cup for another year. Strachan scored first goal for the Rovers, and M'Guire made the game even. A second goal was made for the Rovers out of a scrimmage, and at half time they were a goal ahead. In the second half each side scored once, the Rovers winning by three goals to two.

THE ASSOCIATION CHALLENGE CuP —BLACKBURN OLYMPIC V. OLD ETONIANS.—On eaturday, the deciding trial in this competition came off at Kennington Oval, London. The atten- dance was very large. The opposing teams were the Old Etonian@ and the Blackburn Olympic. and the latter won the honour of holding the cup. In the first half the Old Etonians scored a goal, kicked by Goodhart, but matters were balanced when Massie got the leather through. At the call of " time " the score stood at a goal each, and then the extra half-hour was ! entered upon. A very exciting struggle followed, and at about j fifteen minutes from the call of " time " C.)stley beaded the ball through, and, no further score being made, Blackburn were the winners by two goals to one. The cup was presented by Major Marindin, and Mr. Coddington. M.P. for Blackburn, acknowledged the compliment on behalf of the winners. The Etonians suffered a severe loss through Dunn getting damaged during the first half, but by way of a set-off the Blackburn men had three of their men crippled. It was a gtandly-con- tested trial, and the Blackburn men won by fast play and good condition.

The Convention of Scottish Burghsassembled on Tuesday for the first time since 1704, when there were 41 subjects to be discussed, as against 51 now. The Rev. Joshua Priestley, Wesleyan minister, died at his residEnce in Accrington, on -Monday, aged 73. Mr. Prieitley had teen in the Wesleyan ministry about 43 Years. The Royal Star Theatre and Music Hall, Stockton-on- Tees, was burnt to the ground early on Tuesday morning, and the whole of the scenery and effects destroyed. A tramp who was arrested in Higher Tranmere with 2s 3id in a purse in one of his boots, and a Post Office Savings Bank book in his pocket showing 8s to his credit, was, on Tuesday, sent to gaol for a month, with hard labour, for begging. The annual meeting of the Roman Catholic bishops of England and Wales took place on Tuesday, at the Arch- bishop's house, Westminster, under the presidency of Cardinal Manning. In the evening there was a reception of the Catholic nobility and gentry in town. On Tuesday morning a woman was observed by a police constable in Wapping to throw her child over a bridge into the docks, and then attempt to throw herself after it. The policeman, however, was in time to prevent this, and having procured assistance, rescued the child also. At a convention of the Scottish burghs in Glasgow, on Tuesday afternoon, a motion was carried declaring that it was impossible to govern Scotland satisfactorily by an Eng- lish department of State, and the convention thereof decided to memorialise Parliament to create a separate department to conduct Scotch affairs. An inquiry into charges of drunkenness and immorality preferred against the Rev. E. A. Fitzroy, incumbent of St. Judes's, Liverpool, was held on Wednesday. The evidence was, on the application of Mr. Fitzroy, taken in private. The Commissioners at the close announced that they were of opinion that there was prima facie ground for the institu- tion of further proceedings. An alarming accident to a tramcar occurred on Saturday, at Birkenhead. Or. one of the cars approaching Woodside Ferry the brake did not act, and the vehicle ran down the decline at great speed, knocking over a strong iron pillar in its course. The passengers were much shaken, and one lady had to be taken home in a cab. A gentleman also had a shocking cut on the head. The front of the car was smashed to pieces. Lady Florence Dixie has left " ['he Fishery" and re- turned to her house in Leicestershire. It is stated with every appearance of authority that the Eton gentleman who saw Lady Florence on the afternoon when the mysterious person with the "livid countenance and clenched teeth "is said to have attacked her, is prepared with corroboration of his statement that no attack at all was made on her. His evidence is of the most precise description, and contradicts Lady Florence in every single partlcular. Probably, in the opinion of the public, .enough has been heard of this sub- ject. ALARMING RAILWAY ACCIDENT.-011 Tuesday afternoon, in consequence of the failure of the continuous brake, a special train from London, consisting of fifteen carriages and guard's van, ran through the Midland station, Northampton, and into the shed, forcing the stop blocks out of position, and earring away the end of the shed and dis- placing a large quantity of brickwork in the Warwick Arms, Bridge-street, abutting on the terminus. A quantity of glass was broken and a portion of the debris forced into the smoke room, causing great consternation. Singular to state, none of the passengers felt any shock. SIXPENNY TELEGRBAIS.—We are iniormed that in official circles it is thought that there is little, probability of imme- diate effect being given to the resolution of the House of ' Commons in favour of the reduction in the price of tele- grams. It is pointed out that already the chief lines of communication are almost congested during the busy hours of the day, and that a partial breakdown throws a degree of pressure upon the " good " circuits which is beyond their transmitting power. It is not anticipated that a reduction to sixpence will induce the public to send messages to places in which they have no correspondents, and accord- ingly the increase which may. be laoked for will be in the telegrams addressed to the great commercial centres of the kingdom, which are already in possession of as much work as they can adequately deal with.—Globe. EXTRAORDINARY SPEECH BY AN M.P.—A correspondent writes to the Daily News :—At a time when the Tory party take so great an interest in extra-Parliamentary utterances and are so sensitive of what is said of them by their politi- cal opponents, the following choice specimen of Conserva- tive oratory may be of some interest; it is an extract from a speech delivered at the inaugural banquet of the Norwood Conservative Association by Mr. Grantham, M.P., and Ireported in the Crystal Palace District Times, and is as fol- lows :—" And that young hopeful, that bleating baby, Mr. Herbert Gladstone, that mischief-maker; for him to talk of the malicious character of Her Majesty's Opposition. Who was it who only talked a few weeks ago of giving way still more to the disloyalty of Ireland, pandering to Parnell, Sheridan, and- his followers? And what was the answer to his soft and bleating accents? The answer was the explo- sion at the Government offices last night by Mr. Herbert Gladstone's friends, who had come. out in their true colours and shown the metal they were made of. He (Mr. Gran- tham) thanked them for the attack of last night, because it would show the country what Mr. Chamberlain and his allies I were made of."

PenwatENTenv CONSTITIIENCIEg.—A Parliamentary re- turn issued upon the motion of Sir Charles Dilke, was pub- lished on Monday, showing with respect to each Parlia- mentary constitnency in the United Kingdom the total number of electors on the register now in force. From this it appears that the total of electors in England and Wales is 2,632,223 (966,631 in counties, 1,651,761 in cities and borouebs, and 13,831 in universities); 226,511 in Ireland (164.679 in counties, 57,784 in cities and boroughs, and 4,048 in Dublin University), and 322,967 in Scotland (99,346 in counties, 210,858 in burghs, and 12,763 in uni- versities). The largest county constituency in England is Middlesex (38,373), in Wales, Glamorgan (13,222), in Ire- land, Cork (14,755), and in Scotland, North Lanark (10,949); while the smallest in England is Rutland (1,768), in Wales, Radnor (2,352), in Ireland, Louth (1,999), and in Scotland, Sutherland (340). The largest borough constituency in England is Liverpool (63,436), in Wales the Swansea dis- trict (14,345) ; in Ireland, Belfast (21,086), and in Scotland, Glasgow (63,716). Among the borough constituences of England the six largest are Liverpool (63,436), Birming- ham (63,221), Manchester (52,831), Lambeth (51,064), Leeds (50,675), and Finsbury (48,223); while the six smallest are Marlborough (647), Richmond (721), Knaves- borough (728), Tewkesbury (748), Liskeard (770), and Lymington (817). The three smallest borough'constituen- cies in Wales are Brecon (878), the Radnor district (917), and the Haverfordwest, district (1,495); in Ireland—Portar- lington (138), Kinsale (199), and New Ross (238); and in Scotland—the Wigtown district (1,340), the Wick district (1,687), and-The Haddington district (1,805). THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—If any- thing a feeling of depression prevails in the iron trade. There was a good attendance on 'Change on Tuesday, but so far as business was concerned the market was extremely quiet. Pig-iron meets with an exceedingly slow sale; a few small lois of foundry change hands, but for forge titian- ties there is an almost entire absence of inquiry. Prices nominally are unchanged, but if anything the market is weaker, and for some distinct brands rather less money is being taken. For delivery equal to Manchester, Lanca- shire pig•iron is quoted at 478 6d to 48s, and Lincolnshire brands at 455 6d to 46$ 6d and 475, less 4, for forge and foundry qualities. The finished iron trade also continues quiet. For delivery into the Manchester district quotations remain at about £5 5s to £6 7s 6d per ton for local and North Staffordshire bars.—With a continued fairly good demand for all classes of round coal except some of the inferior sorts, the announcement by the leading Manchester firms with the commencement of the month of a reduction in prices has come upon the market generally as a surprise. The following reductions have been announced by the lead- ing Manchester colliery firms :—Best and seconds coal de- livered in Manchester, Salford, and the surrounding district are reduced 101 per ton; best coal at the Manchester wharves 106 per ton, beat and seconds coal at the Salford yards ICrd per ton; furnace coal, engine coal, and slack de- livered 3d per ton, but not altered at the wharves. The pit prices, with the exception of one or two minor alterations, are practically unchanged from last month. The prices for delivery in Manchester and Salfordewill now average about as under:—Best coal, 12s 6d to 13s 4d; seconds, 10s 10d to Ils 8d; furnace'coal, 8s 9d to 9s 2d; burgy, 78 2d to 7s 7d; and slack, 5s 9d to 6s 3d. It is not improbable that the unsettlement of the market caused Jay the reduction in Manchester coupled with the warmer weather may necessi- tate some corresponding action on the part of colliery firms in other districts. The shipping trade continues dull, with low prices ruling at Garston and Liverpool. • THE Lanonn MARKET.—The labour market generally is

good, and with the improving weather building. operations in London and provinces keep brisk. At the numerous railways and harbour works being constructed work is plentiful, an 3 plenty of navvies are wanted. In mining districts, the "restriction of output" keeps the miners un- settled. In some of the iron districts labour is in demand. At Barnsley, the rolling mills and foundries are well em- ployed; and at Barrow-in-Furness, shipbuilding is brisk. At Birmingham hardware shows a slight improvement. Steel-pen manufacturers and brass founders are busy, and manufacturers of railway iron work are also busy. At Dar- lington, the forge and engineering works are well employed, bat the steel trade is.quiet. At the Hartlepools, the marine engineers and shipbuilders are very busy, and dock labour is increasing. At Sheffield, ironfeunders and marine en- gineers are very active, and miners are fairly employed. In light branches of cutlery - there is plenty of work, but in the electro-plate and file trades work is limited. At Newport (Mon.), the iron works are very busy. At Middlesborough, steel trade is fairly brisk. At Stoke-upon-Trent finished iron is quiet. In South Shropshire there is a fair quantity of work in girder and boiler plates and iron rods and wire.. At Sunderland the foundries, rolling mills, forges, engine works, and shipyards are busy. At Wolverhampton machinery for finished iron is going regularly, and angle and girder makers are well employed. The textile trade do not show much activity. At Bradford spinners are busy; and at Halifax coating manu- facturers are busy. At Huddersfield cheap tweed makers are busy, although the weavers' strike impedes labour. The ribbon weavers at Coventry are agitating for higher and more uniform wages. At Kidderminster spinning machinery is fully engaged, and carpet manufacturers are actively em- ployed. At Leeds worsted-coating makers are working over- time, and makers of thick and thin clothes are busy. At Manchester only regular hours are maintained.- At Notting- ham and Leicester factories are not very busy. The shoe- makers are busy at Stafford, Northampton, Norwich, and even Dublin. Emigration is brisk, and it has extended to the mining districts, and numbers of miners are weekly leav- ing Whitehaven.—The Labour News'

div.head: EXAMINER., SATURDAY. APRIL 7, 1883. WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL,
div.p: THE EXAMINER., SATURDAY. APRIL 7, 1883. WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL,

Arrangements are being made for the visit of 400 repre- sentative British fishermen to the opening of the Inter- national Fisheries Exhibition by the Queen on the 12th May. A meeting of weavers' delegates has resolved to ask the Huddersfield manufacturers to agree to a reference of the wages dispute to arbitration. About 12,030 operatives are at present idle. Letters have been forwarded to Lady Harcourt and Lady Hayter containing pieces of flannel blanket infected with smallpox. The detectives are eudeavouring to trace the authors of this shocking outrage. Petitions were adopted at a meeting held in Manchester, on Tuesday, of delegates representing the North-western Poor-law Conference, against the Poor-law Removal Bill, and in favour of the Maintenance of Children Bill. A fire broke out on Thursday morning in a newsagent's shop at London Wall. One of the inmates had 3 narrow escape by jumping from the first floor window, whereby he hurt his side severely. The Plymouth Radical Association has passed a vote of thanks to Lord Randolph Churchill for opposing the vote to repair the royal palaces, and requests .him to address a gathering of the members. Lord Tollemache, who fell heavily over a dog last Satur- day, has since been confined to his room at Pickforton, suffering from the shock. His lordship was enabled to take, slight exercise on Thursday. morning. The Press Association learns that a Committee of Privi- leges of the Wesleyan Conference is about to meet for the purpose of considering the desirability of petitioning Parlia- ment in opposition to the Affirmation Bill. An anonymous letter has been received by Mr. Coiling- ridge, of the City Press, stating that the offices of that paper vill be blown up on or before the 28th inst.. The communication is in the hands of the police. A girl, 16 years old, was remanded at Westminster; on Thursday, charged with having attempted suicide. She had made an attempt to jump into the Thames, and when rescued declared that she had preViously taken laudanum. A rule was issued on Tuesday by the Queen's Bench, calling upon the proprietors of the Birmingham Gazette to show cause why a criminal information should not be filed against them for an alleged libel on the Attorney- General. At the Cheshire Quarter Sessions, on Monday, the Chair- man (Lord Egerton) was authorized to sign, on. behalf of the Court, a petition in favour of certain clauses being in- serted in the Warrington Tramways Bill for the protection of Warrington Bridge. Reports from the hill districts in Scotland state that the past month was the worst experienced for sheep for many years. Many ewes have died from the severity of the weather and the consequent scarcity of food. Isolated cases of lambing are reported, bat it will not be general till the middle of the month. _

SPECIAL MEETING. A special meeting of the Council was held on Tuesday in the Council Chamber, Town Hall, in pursuance of the pro- visions of the Act of 35th and 36th Victoria, cap. 91, intituled "An Act to authorise the application of funds of municipal corporations, and other governing bodies in certain cases," for the purpose of considering, and (if thought desirable) of passing a resolution to oppose in Par- liament "A Bill to authorise the construction of a ship canal to Manchester, and for other purposes." The Mayor (Councillor Crosfield) presided, and there were present Aldermen Pickmere, Davies, Burgess, Holmes, Harrison, and Kean; Councillors Monks, Sutton, Platt, Wallington, Dixon, Mackie, Bolton, Dakin, Woolfall, Taylor, Ashton, Hutchinson, Burgess, Litton, Sutton, Francornb, Caldwell, Wright, Barker, J. Pierpoint ; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), and T. Longdin (borough surveyor).— About a dozen ratepayers also attended. OPPOSITION TO THE SHIP CANAL BILL. The MAYou pointed out the object of the meeting, and moved the following resolution: "That this Council do oppose in Parliament a Bill authorising the construction of the ship canal to Manchester and for other purposes, and that the Town Clerk be instructed to take all such necessary steps, by petition or otherwise, as may be deemed expedient for the due protection of the rights and interests *of the borough of Warrington, as represented by this Council ; and that the costs, charges, and expenses incurred, in such opposition, be charged upon the borough fund, borough _ _ _

_ At the Bolton Police Court, on Thursday morning, Wm. Hilton, cotton spinner, was charged with employing four women at his factory during the dinner hour. The defence was that the women were cleaning the machinery without the knowledge of the defendant, who had no desire to break the law. Pleading guilty on one charge, a floe and costs amounting to 45s were imposed, and the other cases with-

drawn. The aegnments were concluded on Wednesday in the case of the Tbirlmere Water scheme arbitration, in which the Manchester Corporation sought to set aside the awardof the Arbitrator in favour of the Countess Mary Ossalinsky. Mr. Justice Grove, in delivering judgment, said no ground had been shown upon whi:h the award should be set aside, and therefore the rule ought to be discharged. Mr. Justice Stephen concurred. ILLICIT WHISKY MANUFACTURE.—At the Leek Police Court, on Wednesday, Ann Bailey, Elie tbeth, her daughter, and Abraham Green, of Lask Bridge, near Leek, were con- victed of manufacturing illicit whisky. The elder Bailey was fined £3O, the daughter £5, and Green £l5. Mrs. Bailey pleaded guilty, and stated that she had done it for four years to keep her family respectable and to make up £6OO of which her late husband had robbed her. A woman named Lewis died in Clatterbridge Workhouse on Thursday evening, from dreadfel injuries sustained from burns. Deceased, who lived at Neston, was heard screaming, and on the neighbours hersting in the door she was found enveloped in flames, with a paraffin lamp upset at her side. The fire was extinguished, bat not before shocking injuries had been sustained to her arms, legs, and side. The woman was removed to Cletterbridge Workhouse, where she suc- cumbed as above. The notorious " Mary Ann," which created such a sensa- tion in Sheffield some years ago, has appeared at Bolton. On Thursday n)orning, before the Bolton magistrates, a youth named John Hargreaves was charged with cutting six cotton bands connected with Messts. Lord, Hampson, and Lord's spinning mill. The prisoner had cut the bands from spite against the firm, who refused to pay him after leaving without notice. He was discharged on promising to , pay the costs. A POLICEMAN SENT TO PRISON.—At Leicestershire Ses- sions, on Tuesday, before Sir Henry Halford, Thomas Wm. Stevens, a policeman, was indicted for obtaining, at Lutter- worth, in October last, several sums of money by pretend- ing that be had become entitled to some money and the Hare and Hounds Inn, at High Wycombe, Buckingham- shire. The prisoner asserted that be required the money to pay certain costs in order to get possession of the property. He was sentenced to three months' hard labour. The funeral of Mr. John Brown took place at noon on Thursday, the body being removed from the deceased's re- sidence near Baltnoral, to Craithe Kirkvard. There were frequent showers during the morning, but the rain ceased before the time fixed for the interment. The attendance was very large, the whole of the tenantry on the Royal estates of Balmoral, Abergillie, and Barhhill being present, whilst large numbers also attended from Braemar, Ballater, and the properties of Invercauld and Glenmuick. A TWIN DAY•SALOON RAILWAY CARRIAGE. —The London and North-Western Railway CArmany have just added tcr the train accommodation in the service between Manchester and the metrbpolis, a new drawing-room car- riage of a form not hitherth in use on this line. Two car- riages joined together and connected by a gangway make practically one carriage. One portion forms a saloon for ladies and parties, and the other an ordinary saloon. In the latter there is a gentlemen's smokeroom. The whole car- riage is beautifully fitted up, and there is every convenience provided, even to electric communication with the atten- dant. Ordinary first-class fares are charged. THE SPLIT AMONGST GOOD TEMPLARS.—The committee appointed at the Good Templar Conference at Gloucester to inquire into the libel case arising cut of the negro question having reported, the Grand Lodge has adopted their report as a manifesto, in which it isistated that the arbitration de- cision of Mr. A. M. Sullivan bears no relation to the Grand Lodge beyond the fact of five of its members being joined as defendants, and that Mr. Sullivan's observations were volunteered on the Charter suit, which was not be- fore him. The manifesto reiterates that the Grand Lodge is willing to re-unite when its opponents have secured in America equality in the r!ghl of admission to the Order. , THE PROPOSED TAX ON VISITORS TO THE ISLE OP,MAN. —lnfluence is being brought to bear upon the Board of Trade and the governing authorities of the Isle of Man against a proposal to increase the revenue for harbour pur- poses by means of a duty not exceeding 3d. for every pas- senger arriving at or departing from Douglas. The steam- packet authorities and the boarding-house keepers and hotel proprietors at that port, numbering 418, have signed a memorial against this proposal, and it has been presented to Mr. Hclms, M.P., Parliamentary Secretary of the Board of Trade. Another deputation on the same subject from the traders of Douglas will wait upon the Lieutenant Governor of the island.

COUNTY RATES IN ENGLAND.—A parliamentary return has been issued, giving an abstract of the countylreasurers' accounts for the year ended Lady Day, 1882. The memo- randum prefixed to the summary states that thete has been an increase of 8.2 per cent. in receipts and of 21 in ex- penditure.over the figures for the previous year. Dining the year the valuation for county rates amounted to .E 119,672,612 an incfease of £615,773, and that for police rates to £76,522,388, an increase of £766,530. The total re- ceipts amounted to 3,248,081, an increafle of £246,021; the total of loc it and imperial taxation being £2.469,261, an increase of £175,281. The' total expenditure was £3,063,182, an increass of £79,531. The , average rate in the pound for county rate in all England was 2 9-16 d. for the year 1881-2, and for police rate 11. The loans raised on the security of the rates, and outstanding against the county authorities at Lady Day, 1882, amounted to £3,112,185. ELOPEMENT OF A LIVERPOOL BROKER.—A flutter of excitement has been caused on the Liverpool Exchange by the disclosures of an extraordinary escapade on the part of a retired Liverpool cotton broker, on theaady side of 60, who up to recently had been a partner in one of the oldest firms in the bwiness. It would appear that, during his business visits to Manchester and the district, this gay Lothario made the acquaintance of a dashing barmaid in one of the many restaurants which are to be found in the neighbourhood of the Manchester Exchange. The acquaint- ance had subsisted for some time, and it culminated a few days ago in the flight of the pair. The course thus taken does not appear to have been hastily resolved on as the gentleman placed all his affairs in proper order, and in a letter to his wife announcing his flight he told her not to think any more of him, as he had quite made up his mind to stay abroad with his young inamorata. The frequenters of 'Change were naturally shocked at the news, as he seemed to be quite a staid, stay-at-home husband and father. He has a grown up family, one son being a partner in the firm to which the father once belonged. CAMBRIDGE LOCAL ExamlNATtorts.—The Syndicate appointed by the Senate to conduct the local examinations have just issued their 25th annual report of the examina- tions conducted at the various centres in December last, the

class list of which was published on the 25th February. The examinations were held in December at 118 centres for boys and 104 for girls. It appears that In 1878 there were entered 3,329 junior boys, 1,483 junior girls, 626 senior . boys, and 997 senior girls, making a total of 6,43. In 1882 the corresponding figures were 3,926 junior boys, 1,793 junior girls, 648 senior boys, and 1,273 senior girls—total, 7,640. In 1882, of the 3,668 junior boys examined 316 per cent passed in honours, 41 per cent ngt in honours, making a total passed per cent of 72.6; the failures being 274 per cent. Of the 1,740 junior girls examined 23.6 passed in honours, 47.9 not in honours: the total number passed was 715, while the total failurzs were 28.5. Of the 605 senior boys examined 26 per cent passed in honours, 317 per cent not in honours-57'7 per cent total passes, while , the total failures were 42 3 per cent. Of the 1,338 senior girls examined 13 per cent passed in honour, 48 per cent passed not in honours. 'The total passed was 50 per cent, while the total failures were 44 per dent.
