THE SANITARY COMMITTEE AND THE DEPUTATIONS. The proceedings of the committee were adopted. _. . . .

FINANCE. The proceedings of the Finance Committee were opposed, and a resolution was passed calling upon the overseers of the township of Warrington, Latchford. and Theheall to contribute their proportions of £3,493 14s. 3d. on borough rate account within 30 days. Resolutions sanctioning an improvement rate of is. 31. in the £, and a sewer rate of 21. in the £, were also agreed to. A statement was made that this half year the rates are lower. This concluded the business. THE FENIAN APPREHENSIONS AT ST. HELENS AND LIVERPOOL. THE PRISONERS BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. On Saturday morning the two men in custody of the Liverpool police were unexpectedly brought up before Mr. Raffles, at the Dale-street Police Court. There were only a few persons in court. The names of the men were given as Patrick Flannigan, aged 31, and Dennis Deasey, aged 26. Mr. Marks prosecuted, and on the bench with Mr. Raffles were Col. Ford, her Majesty's Inspector of Explosives, and Captain Nott Bower, the head constable. Dr. Campbell Brown, the public analyst, was also in court. The prisoners were charged with knowingly having in thebe possession dangerous explosive substances with intent to commit a felony. Mr. Marks said the case was only in a very initiatory stage at present, and he would simply call evidence as to the find- ing of the articles in question, and he would ask Colonel 11 Ford to state that in his opinion they were explosives which were unauthorised and illegal. Inspector Marsh, sworn, said: At seven o'clock on the night of Wednesday, the 28th inst., I, in company with De- tectives Canning and Curran, were at. the Landing-stage, watching the arrival of the Cork steamer. The boat arrived, and 10 minutes after the 'gangway was thrown across I saw Deasey, come ashore. He spoke to a badge porter, and they both returned to the boat. They went to the fore part of the vessel, and they returned to the stage in two minutes, the porter carrying a box and Deasey walking by his side. It was a small wooden box, about 18 inches by 12 inches. I have not measured it. They left the stage and went along to the Waterloo Dockgate. We followed. After going a short distance I stopped them close to the Waterloo Dock gate. I said to Deasey, "What have you got in this box?" He replied, "Cattle food." I saw it was heavy, from the manner in which the porter was carrying it. I replied, "It seems heavy for cattle food; let nan see it." I took him to the police hut close by, and had the box brought in as well. The box was locked, and tied down with cord. I sent for a cab. I told him I should take him and the box to the head office to be examined. He said," I was engaged by a man named Murphy, who is a commercial traveller, to bring this .box to Liverpool. Murphy led me to believe he was a traveller in the cattle food line." I then took him to the Detective Office. At the Detective Office the box was opened. The contents were subsequently submitted to Dr. Campbell Brown for analysis. He examined them at the Detective Office. I searched Deasey. These two documents (produced) were found in his possession. I also found on him a key which fits the box. He said the man Murphy was to meet him at the Landing-stage. This was said in the police•court. I charged the two prisoners this morning, and they made no reply. Samuel Johnson, detective officer, said :—On Wednesday night I went to Sutton, St. Helens' with Sergeant Canning. We met the prisoner Flannigan. We went to 24, Convent- road, where Flannigan lodged. In his room was found a box, which was locked. Canning told Flannigan that we were going to examine his box. He gave us a key, and the box was unlocked in prisoner's presence. Inside the box we found a black leather bag. It was locked. I asked Flannigan if be had a key. He showed me a key attached to the same ring as the box key. We opened the bag. In the bag we found a small tin canister. In the canister was a six-chambered revolver, (loaded), forty-one cartridges' and a false beard and moustache all in one. Sub- sequently in a box was found a bottle containing some fluid. He brought all the things be men- tioned to Liverpool. On finding the canister tesked him what the stuff was for, and he replied it was tooth powder. (Laughter.) He said the liquid in the bottle was what he had been taking a few drops of in water for the liver com- plaint. (Laughter.) On arriving in Liverpool we handed all the articles I have mentioned to Dr. Campbell Brown for analysis.—The prisoner Flannigan (to witness) : Did you bring all that material with you when you left Sutton? Witness: All but the bottle.—And where did you leave the bottle? Inside your bag, and I went on the following day for it.—Did you find any letters or correspondence in the box? There were several letters.—Did you examine them all ? Yes.—Were they of any consequence? No,they were letters from friends. Dr. Campbell Brown, public analyst, sworn, said :—At a quarter-past eight o'clock on Wednesday nicht I was called to the Detective Office, and was shown a large wooden box, containing several things which I was told to examine. I found two tin cases carefully stitched in canvas. I un- stitched the canvas, and opened one of the cases filled with a highly explosive substance. I also found other substances of an explosive character, and some instruments, and took some samples, and directed the removal of the rest to a place of safety. I wes subsequently shown a tin canister and a bottle of fluid by Detective Johnson. They were of the same as the other ingredients found in the box. They are precisely of the same nature, and taken together they are also highly explosive. The explosives I found could not, all taken in connection with each other, be used for any legal purpose.—The prisoner Flannigan (to witness).— And what is the name of that substance which you found? (Laughter).—Witness.—l don't think I can answer that question. Mr. Raffles.—l don't know what he wants to know. Mr. Marks.—He wants to know the name of the substance which Dr. Campbell Brown found in his (prisoner's) box. Prisoner.—What is the name of the substance that you found in my box ?—Witneee : Oil of vitriol,—Prisoner: And how do you mean to say that it is explosive P—Wit- ness : I say that when all the ingredients are mixed to- gether they do explode. No doubt you know. (Laughter.)— Prisoner : I know nothing at all about it. Deasey said he had no questions to ask at present. By Flannigan.—The fluid in the bottle was oil of vitriol. Colonel Arthur Ford, .of the Royal Artillery, and her Majesty's inspector of explosives, sworn, said e-4 have not as yet had an opportunity of making an ex- amination of these articles referreil to myself, but I am aware of the results of Pr. Campbell Brown's analysis. I should class explosives as authorised and unauthorised. The explosive described by Dr. Brown is unauthorised, and could not be legally used or even kept for private use. The name of the explosive is lignine-dynamite. —Flannigan: Is that a similar scrt of stuff that was used at the Houses of Parliament ? (Laughter.) The evidence was then read over, and prisoners were re- manded for a week. The prisoners during the inquiry appeared to treat the matter in :t jocular way, and smiled and laughed frequently. DESCRIPTION OF THE PRISONERS. Flannigan is a man of abut middle height, and is clad in an old and odd suit of clothes, and wears a thick-look- ing muffler around his neck. There is no hair on his face, neither does he appear to be over intelligent. Deasey, the younger of the two, like Flannigan, possesses neither moustache, beard, nor whiskers. He seems to be smarter than his fellow prisoner, and is taller and of stouter build, being about sft. 91n. or sft. 10in, in height. He is clad in a long brown overcoat, and appears altogether to have been ;n a more comfortable condition of life than Flannigan.

A serious fire occurred on Wednesday morning in the large spice mills of Messrs. Wright, Crossley, and Co., Liverpool. TRA3I CAR ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS.—On Monday, a little girl named Mary Lancaster, who lives with her parents in Park-road, Parr, was dreadfully hurt by a tram car which runs between St. Helens and illydock. It apped,rs that the child, who is only four years of age, was playing in the street, and unheedingly run in front of the car when in motion. She was knocked down and run over, and injured so seriously that her left arm was nearly severed from the body and had to be amputated. The left leg was also very badly crushed.

A PAIR or SIRENS. Two women, named Catherine Carey and Maria Lee, were on Thursday charged at the St. Helens Police Court, with having stolen a muffler and hand- kerchief, the property of a young man, James Holmes, of 24, Liverpool-street, on Tuesday.—lt appeared that the pro- secutor had met the two prisoners in company with a man named Donoghue, and they invited him tos Donoghue's house. He went there, and whlst there he bad some beer. He then fell asleep and remained asleep till he was awakened by his mother, who had come to seek him, about one o'cl?ck on Wednesday morning. The articles named were missing and the prisoners gone. Evidence was also given to show that the articles had been seen in the possession of Carey, and were afterwards pawned by Lee.—They were both cora- , mitted for trial at the sessions.

div.head: ORDINARY MEETING.
div.p: ORDINARY MEETING.
The business of the ordinary monthly meeting of the Council was then proceeded with, the Mayor still presiding, and the same members and officials being present.
THE BUILDING BYE-LAWS.----THE LIGHTING OF THE BOROUGH.

Councillor PLATT, in moving the confirmation of the pro- ceedings of the Street Improvement and Lighting Commit- tee, drew attention to the resolution of the committee instructing the Town Clerk and Borough Surveyor to revise the building bye-laws, and said it had been found from time to time that some of the bye-laws, as at present drafted, failed of their effect, and that others were unworkable. It was therefore the intention of the Street Improvement Committee to carefully go into the matter and submit to the Council at some future time amended bye-laws. Respecting the resolution containing the removal of the circus in Sankey-street, he might say that since that resolution was passed the Street Improvement Committee had had a satis- factory guarantee that the circus would be conducted in a decent and orderly manner, and that the owner would pull it down at any time when called upon after two months' notice, therefore the committee proposed that the resolution in favour of pulling it down at once should be rescinded. Councillor BARKER seconded the confirmation of the proceedings.

THE ATHLETIC TOURNAMENT AT ST. HELENS.—An enter- taininent of more than usual attractiveness is advertised to take place in Culeen's Circus, ivorth-road, St. Helens, on Monday evening. This is a grand athletic tournament to be given by the members of the Liverpool Gymnasium, who are admitted on all hands to be a fine body of athletes, and highly proficient in the various exercises they propcse to go through; and they will also be assisted by local bicycle riders, dzc. Mr. T. D. McKenzie will—as a result of a chal- lenge to him which appeared in the Athleac News from Mr. J. Maude—contest with that expert for a prize of a silver lever hunting watch, presented by Mr. Alexander, of Liver- pool, a contest which of itself will be of surpassing interest to local bicyclists.

FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT Al' ST. HELENS. On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. I'. W. Baker, county coroner, held an inquest at the Griffin Inn, Peasley Cross, St. Helens, en the body of Tereuce Brennan, aged 25 years, who lived in St. Thomas's-street, and was employed as a fireman in the Little Delf Mine, belonging to the St. Helens •Collieries Company. Mr. F. France, manager, represented Messrs. Pilkington Bros. From the evidence it appeared:that Ideceased was assisting to bring waggons up the brow, al- though it was not his duty. Several waggons had gone to the top and was bringing another on to the line, having his back to the waggons which had gone up, when the hook of the last waggon snapped, and it ran down some 30 yards and crushed deceased against the wagg)n with which he was engaged. When lifted up, it was found he had sus- tained very serious injuries, his right leg and two ribs having been broken, and his thigh- shockingly lacerated. He lost a large quantity of blood before medical assistance could be obtained. After being attended to at the Cottage Hospital hopes were entertained of his recovery, but he gradually sank, and died on Saturday last. The hook was produced at the inquest, and it was found that there was a defect in the metal which it was impossib.e to see from the outside. it was stated that the books and chains were regularly examined, and the Coroner and jury considered there was no blame attributable to anyone, and deceased's relations said he told them before bis death that no one was to blame. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

Present: Mr. John Ashton (in the chair), the Rev. J. they have produced a result the very reverse. Lockwood, Messrs. Derbyshire, Andrews, Rigby, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. 'Linaker (assistant clerk). Medical Officer's Report: It was decided on the motion of Mr. An- drews, seconded, by Mr. Lockwood, that the medical officer's report should be printed.--The Feolshant Sewerage Scheme: A letter was read from Mr. Bancroft acknowledging the re- ceipt of a communication from the Board enclosing a copy of a resolution passed by the authority at a meeting held on the 30th inst., requesting him to negotiate with the owners of lands and easements required by the scheme. He should be happy to undertake the duty, and should like to receive from them the names and addresses of the owners and where it is proposed constructing the reservoir—Men-holes to Main-sewers at Frodshani : The Inspector reported that he had caused the valves at Frodsham sewerage ()titian works, and the manholes to main sewers to be examined and cleansed, and the whole was now in good working order.— Water Supply to Cottages in Norley : The Inspector re- ported that various cottages situate near Hatchmore's, Norley, were without a water supply, and he wished to know in what position the Authority stood with respect to such cottages being supplied from the Liverpool mains which pass most of them.—The Cleik stated that they could not he supplied from the mains, and the Inspector said he would , prepare a detailed report upon the matter for the next meet- lug—This was all the business of interest. ! ROBERTS Jim DOYLE AT RUNCORN.—These amateur reciters and character impersonators gave a performance in Runcorn Public Hall, with the object of clearing off the debt incurred by the Young Men's Christian Association in giving the treat to poor children some months ago. Notwith- standing the -strenuous exertions made to attract a crowded , audience, the hall was not more than half filled, and, we regret to say, the debt will Kill remain a burden to the asso- ciation. The entertainment was an enjoyable one. Mr. W. H. Roberts, who is a native of Runcorn, is a young man of talent, and in his recitations and songs created a most , favourable impression. Of his recitations we would single out " The dream of Eugene Aram" as a fine piece of elo- . cutionary power, although, perhaps, slightly burdened with an excess of melo-dramatic action. The seed° in the Mer- chant of Venice, where Antonio negotiates a loan from Shy- lock, was recited, and Mr. Roberts took the part of Shylock , with great ability, , introducing the mannerisms ,of Henry Trying. He .scored a success in the Comical song "The careful man," and again as ; the street stab, when he ,sang "The little scrub." Mr. Doyle is entitled to a high rank as a reciter. He gave "In the workhouse" and "The life-boat" with a pathos and power which excited the eager interest of his audience, and he was loudly applauded. 'His impersonation of "Police- 1 man CXI." chimed in with the popular humour, and created I much amusement. Messrs. Roberts and Doyle conjoined In; "The wily eloper," an extravaganza, which concluded the I evening's entertainment. It was a very laughable perform- ance, and the topical song it embraced gave several capital local hits. During the evening the National School brass band performed selections of music in good style. Mr. War- burton presided at the piano. RUNCORN BOAR. D OF GUARDIANS.-0G Tuesday the usual meeting of this board was held at the Dutton Work- house. Mr. John Ashton presided, and there were present the Rev. G. Lockwood; Messrs. Derbyshire, Stokes, Andrews, Norman, Rigby, Wallington, Handley, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk).— Workhouse , Drainage Committee : The report of this committee was; adopted on the motion of Mr. Derbyshire, seconded by Mr. Thomas Norman.—The Union Books: The committee re- commended that the room in the workhouse known as the old nursery, was a suitable place for the storage of the union books, provided a movable double rack be placed in the middle.—The report was adopted, as was also% motion that the books be brought to the Boardroom and classified.— The Election: On the motion a- Mr. Handley, it was decided that the remuneration of the Clerk as returning officer should be £2O as before.—Attendance of Guardians: The following are the general attendances of the Guardians ; for the year-25 meetings. Mr. CHILDERS, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, introduced his first budget last night, and we venture to think it will be received with unqualified satisfaction by the country. Very little of a startling character was expected, for the reason, it was well known, that the state of the national finances could not permit of much being set aside in relief of taxation ; but Mr. CHILDE.RS had a surprise in store which even the most ardent Ministerialist did not dare to hope for. The revenue from all sources for the past year, we are told has amounted to £89.004,000,. and the expendi.:ure has been £88,906,000, so that there is a clear surplus of £98,000. Ttis satisfactory to know that under every head with, we believe, only one exception, the revenue has steadily increased; and indeed, 'when we reflct that it is in the receipts .from wine, spirits. and beer, there is a diminished revenue, there is cause for congratulation, for that points to a spread of temperance. It ought to be borne in mind, too, that this surplus of £98,000 is secured by the present Government after defraying a part of the war legacies left by their predecessors, and wholly covering the cost of the Egyptian campaign. Another point worthy of note is this: That during the six years' tenure of office of Lord Beaconsfield £i8,160,000 of debt was paid off, equal to L 3,117,000 per year; while during the three years which the present Government has been in office £z0.517,000 has been liquidated, equal to £6,839,000 a year. This year the reduction will be a little over £8,000,000. The esti- mated expenditure for the current year:is £85,789,000, and the receipts without any reduction of taxation are placed at £BB4Bojooo, so that should the expenditure be kept within the estimate and the receipts no less than are anticipated, there will be in April next a disposable surplus of £z,691,000. , In view of this the rid. put on the income tax last year to meet the Egyptian war ex- penses is to be removed; in addition, £170,000 is to be set aside to enable six- penny telegrams to be introduced; the rail- way passenger duty on all fares not exceed- ing one penny per mile is to be abolished, and the tax on urban traffic reduced to two per cent. ; a slight reduction is to be made on the duty upon tobacco and snuff; and there is to be a partial remission of the duty on gold and silver plate. It is intended ulti- mately to repeal the duty on these articles altogether. Such, in brief, is the sum and substance of the budget. It gives another instance of the wise economy practised by Liberal Chancellors of the Exchequer, it more than Justifies Mr. CHILDERS' recent appoint- ment to this important post, and it com- pletely disarms adver!, criticism of any moment from the Opposition. It will also Jo much to sustain the Government in the confidence of the country.

WIDNES CHOILIL Socrnry.---This society's last concert of the season will take place on Thursday next, when Mac- Mar-day" and Rossini's " Stabat Mater" will b p rformed. The artistes will be Miss Emily Stewart, Mis- Frances Armstrong, Mr. Arthur Tuer, and Mr. Morreq.

RUNCORN VOLUNTEER CLOTHING CONTRACT.—In the competition for this contract, Messrs. Unsworth Bros., of High-street, were the successful competitors. TEMPERANCE LECTURE.—On Thursday evening ' Mr. Touchstone, of Manchester, delivered a lecture in the Voluu- unteer Hall, under the auspices of the Church of England Temperance Society. His subject was "Public-house signs." The Rev. J. Wright-Williams presided, and there was a good attendance. HALTON PARISH CHURCH CHOIR.—In aid of the funds of thilebody a successful miscellaneous entertainment was given in the Girls' School-room on Tuesday evening, Mr. Joseph Stokes occupying the cl:air. The vocalists were Miss Wright, Miss Parry, Miss Grounds, Messrs. F. Fair- hurst, F. Nickson, R. Morris, and Rooke. Miss Jukes accom- panied, and performed a selection. DESTROYING PROPERTY IN WIDNES. Yesterday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. John Brock and Mr. G. Pilkington, Patrick McCabe and John Wall, youths about 17 years of age, were charged with being upon the premises of Edward Percy, Gorsey-lane, Widnes, for an unlawful purpose. It appeared that Percy locked up the premises on Monday last, but en Thursday the prisoners effected an entrance, and were found in the hayloft of the stable. The flooring of this place had been broken up and part of it re- moved.—P.C. Noble and the prosecutor proved the case.— McCabe, who had been several times previously convicted, was sentenced to six weeks'imprisonment with hard labour, and Wall was sent to gaol for 14 days. & NEGLECT OF FAMILY.—On WeeThesday, at the Widnes Petty Sessions, Joseph Walsh was charged with deserting his wife and family, whereby they became chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union.—Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk to the Guardians), who prosecuted, stated that for some time the prisoner was employed by the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company. Though not in receipt of large wages, he appeared to have sufficient to support his wife and family. Work, however, became slack, and one day in March the defendant tcld his wife that if he did not return by& o'clock that night she need not expect him. He did not return, and from that time made no provision for his wife and children, and made no enquiries concerning them. Mr. Scannel, the relieving officer, visited the house where the woman and her children were, and found them in such a destitute condition that be deemed it necessary to have them removed to the Work- house, where the now were. Men, especially in the Widnes district, thought that if they happened to be out of work it was perfectly natural and proper for them to leave their wives and families to the care of the ratepayers.—Mr. Scannel, relieving officer for the Widnes district, proved the facts.—The Bench sent the defendant to gaol for a month.

iThe Queen, who has not yet sufficiently recovered from i her recent accident to be able to walk, took carriage exercise yesterday morning. On Thursday evening, in Burnley, a child 19 months old, daughter of George Strutt, a weaver, took from a table one of the pills intended for its sick mother, and died soon after from narcotic poisoning. A Renter's despatch, dated Cape Coast Castle, March 19, states.:—The report is confirmed that the King of Ashantee has virtually abdicated, and a messenger is now stated to be on his way to inform Sir Samuel Robe, governor of the Gold Coast, of the fact. Mr. Alfred Giles, Conservative, was nominated yesterday - for the vacancy at Southampton, and was returned un- opposed. He was proposed by Mr. G. Dunlop, cbairmrin of the Conservative party, and many others. The sheriff sat from 10 till 12 to receive nominations, and though there were some talk of a labour candidate, no one but Mr. Giles was nominated. A woman named Ferguson is now in Liverpool Work- house under police surveillance. She was observed, oa Thursday night, to go down the steps leading to the Onal bank having in her arms a child, twelve months old, and leading another about two years old. She threw the elder child.. into the canal and was leaping in with the baby, when a man seized her. After a desperate struggle she was overpowered, the child was rescued. and all were taken to the workhouse. The woman is apparently temporarily I insane.

Henry Brown, 21 years of age, committed suicide in a most determined manner at Burnlev, en Thursday night. The deceased had been in a desponding state of mind since the death of his father, a month ago, and on Thursday pur— chased a sixpenny packet of vermin-killer, stating that he wanted it to destroy some mice. He swallowed the poison in the st:c..et, and told two young men what he had done, at the same time throwing to them the empty packet. The young man expired soon afterwards.

ASHLEY, replying to Lord John Manners, said the agent of tile Transvaal Government had arrived in London, and had asked for an -interview at the Colonial Office.—Mr. GLADSTONE said no negotiations were in progress with-Dr. Jorriesen, as the representative of the Transvaal Government. The Government did not yet know the precise object of the gentleman's visit. It was not necessary that all negotiations should be conducted through the High Commissioners. Sir IL Robinson would be in this Country in May next, and would be in a position to give the Government assistance on the subject. EXPLOSIVES —Sir W. HARCOURT gave notice that on Monday he should ask- leave to iutroduce a bill to amend the law with respect to the possession of explosives. (Loud cheering.) He should ask for postponing the orders of the day in order that the bill might be considered and passed through all its stages without delay. Had they been firing at French or Germans they would not have coins back with the flying colours they did. Ile condemned, at the cost of millions, building largeironclads, any one of which might be sunk by little torpedo boats, while science was in doubt as to the best steps to construct and guys to arm them. He advised the Government to curtail the dock- yard expenditure, to maks less, to trust more to the open market, and only to buy what they wanted. Ho urgcl • the House to make a bold and determined stand against the present extravagant expenditure by adopting his reso- lution. He joined issue with the hon. member on many of the large outlays he so strongly denounced, and notably the abolition of purchase. div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The Monthly meeting was held at the Board Offices, Bridgewater-street, on Wednesday morning. Mr. John Simpson presided, and there were present—The R3V. Father Pennelly, Messrs. Peter Briscoe, Thomas Norman, James Pritchard, and F. Rigby. • FEVAR AND SCHOOL CHILDREN. THE COMMISSIONERS_ CONDUCT CRITICISED.

The CLERK read a lettertdated the 19th March, from Mr. W. Brookes, secretary to the Improvement Commissioners, stating that owing to the continued prevalence of scarlet fever, the Sanitary Committee strongly recommended that no child be admitted or re-admitted to school after an attack of that disease without the certificate of a duly qualified medical man that the child has quite recovered.— Mr. NORMAN remarked that the medical officer of health pressed very hard for this suggestion to be carried out.—Mr. PRITCHARD : In cases of scarlet fever it very frequently occurs that poor people do not call in a medical man. I have heard the visitor state that, and how are we to apply the suggestion to cases of that sort P—Mr. NORMAN said the Board had nothing to do with them if they could not find them out; but in a case where a child had been under a medical man, the latter ought to give a certificate before. that child commenced to mix with others at school.—The CHAIRMAN : I daresay it is desirable.—Mr. NORMAN said Dr. MacDougall was present at the meeting of the commit- tee where that letter was read, and he stated it was a very necessary precaution.—The CLERK: Will they grant certi- ficates free of charge?—Mt. NORMAN: I think so.—The CLERK remarked that when the question of scarlet fever came up before, he mentioned the case of a Woman moving her beds and furniture from one end of the town to the other without let or hindrance, when she had scarlet fever in her house.—The CHAIRMAN pointed out that there was also at the same time a chaff bed thrown on a waste , heap.—The CLERK said he ventured to say that such an I offence was punishable. This had been abundantly proved over and over again, and many people had been punished I since that day in Liverpool, London, and other large towns ; for carelessness, which was really caution as compared with j the case of the chaff bed and the other he had mentioned.? It appeared to him that the eanitary Authority. should do : something in the way of inspecting cases of fever, and really put some restriction upon houses that were infected. I At present householders seemed to move about as they liked, taking fever from one end of the school district to the , other.—The CHAIRMAN concurred. People left cottages, I and other people entered them, without any notice being ' taken of the removals.—The CLERK stated that the Board ; of Commissioners had no system of reporting the cases. The cases came under the notice of the Sanitary Authority ' in a casual way; they had no exhaustive routine which would show that the fever was abating, increasing, or stand- ing still.—Mr.Nonmarr: Oh, yes. Mr. Barker looks after that.—The CLER.K : I am ignorant of, the method;.but I can eay the results are casual.—Mr. NORMAN: In every case , where there is sickness disinfectants are sent every day. Old Joseph is kept purposely to take those disinfect- ants up and down. The CLERK : But how do you know that szarletfever obtains in various places ? Mr. NORMAN: Of course, we get to know through our medical officer.—The CHAIMAN: You must remember that , it is not compulsory to notify cases of scarlet fever.— 1 Father FENNELLT : I don't think I have a case amongst my people. Of course there is a few cases now and again.— • Mr. NORMAN observed that the disease originated in New- town and then spread to Duke's Field. where it was chiefly confined at the present time.—The CLEinK said the sage he spoke of, which never came under the notice of the Sanitary Authority, was merely casually reported to him by Bowyer. At the time of the removal a child was dead or had only just been buried.—Mr. NORMAN': When it was reported to Mr. Barker he said he knew all about it. He didn't , know all about it,until it took place I dare say. (Laugh- ter.)—The CLERK said if Mr. Barker knew all about it, It I was a clear case to report, not, however, through the ' channel of the School Board, and the delinquents ought to , have been punished. It teemed to him that the Commis- sioners were grappling with the disease at the wrong end ,in asking for these certificates. He should prefer to grapple with the disease at its inception, and not when the children ' were in the peeling state. The recommendation of the , Commissioners was very valuable, but it would be very much more 'valuable if they had some systematic way of stamping out the fever.—ln answer to several questions, the CHAIRMAN said the Brunswick School managers had received intimation of the matter, and the teachers understood that they had not to admit children without a certificate.,.-The UERK asked how they were to know that the .children were ill of scarlet fever. The CHAIRMAN thought theleachers would quickly learn.- -The CLERK remarked that if all these elaborate precau- tions were to be taken to prevent children going to school without a certificate, it was desirable that the teachers should know which children had had scarlet fever by means of a register of some kind.—Rev. Father FMNBLLY said the teachers were well acquainted with their own scholars, and would take care to know when they were ill, and not allow them to return until perfectly recovered —The CLERK: They have no means of knowing. If a parent wishes to keep a child away from school, she simply says the child has got scarlet fever.—Rev. Father FENNELLY said this deception could coon be detected by means of the other children in the school.—Mr. NORMAN: .Oh Yes.—Rev. Father FENNELLY : If the children have the 'fever the par- ents will keep them at home as long as theysan. There is no danger at all.—The CLERK: It is not at all an unusual thing for the parents to eay that a child has got the scarlet fever, when it has no illness at all.—Mr. IConmeN: That will'hoon find ite level —lt was decided to forward a copy of the letter to the teachers and ask them to act in accor- dance with the saiggeetion which it contained.
FINA.NCE.

The CLERK said the Board had a balance in the bank of £156; but accounts amounting to £56 to be paid that day reduced it to £lOO. at had been found convenient to draw half-yearly f.om the overseers the sum of £260, and have a talance to work upon. In one case the Board drew the balance rather close, and they had their knuehles rapped. —Mr. NORMAN: A precept of over £2OO will be too much if we have £lOO already.—The CLERK said so far as the ratepayers were concerned it did not make a halfpenny worth of difference.—lt was resolved to issue a precept upon the overseers for £2OO.

div.head: PROJECTED TRUANT SCHOOL.
div.p: PROJECTED TRUANT SCHOOL.

A communication was read from Shrewsbury School Board inviting a representative to attend a meeting of School Boards on May Ist, to discues the question of establishing a truant school.—lt was unanimously decided that the .21erk should attend on behalf of the Board.

div.head: AN APPOINTMENT.
div.p: AN APPOINTMENT.
On the motion of Mr. NORIIAN, seconded by Mr. PRIT- CHARD, Samuel inglefield was appointed to succeed G. Sanders as assistant school attendance officer. VISITOR'S REPORT.

Returns from the public elementary schools for March, 1883 :—Certified government accommodation, 2,716; total number on the rolls, 2,937; number on the rolls correspond- ing period of last year, 2,818; increase in the number on the rolls, 119; total average attendance, 2,1386; average attendance corresponding period of last year, 20924; in- crease in average attendance, 46.1; average attendance for the year 1874. 1,252; increase in average attendance as com- pared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board, 8866; accommodation in excess of average attend- ance, 577.4; number on the rolls in excess of accommoda- tion, 221; number in attendance at private adventure schools under 9d. per week, 76. In the return for the past month I have still to report a decrease in the attendance of infants, The cold and inclement weather has prevented many chil- dren from attending school regularly; severe cold, s.)re throats, and whooping cough are the principal reasons given for their non-attendance. Fever is still very prevalent, and several fresh cases have come under my notice during the past month. since the last meeting of. the Board I have taken proceedings against 18 parents ordered to be dealt with for contravention of the bye-laws and disobedience of attend- ance orders. In 17 cases convictions were granted, and tbe usual flne r..sf ss. imposed.

div.head: MEDIC-AL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: MEDIC-AL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The MEDICAL OFFICER (Dr. Mouritz) in his monthly report, stated that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 36, represent- ing a death rate of 28 per 1,000 per annum. Of the above deaths 19 were due to lung affections; and abdominal, brain, and scarlatina diseises accounted for three each. Sixteen deaths occurred among children five -years and under, and ten one year and under. .
THE BEASLEY BUSINESS AGAIN. THREATENED AcrioN FOR CONTEMPT.

The CHAIRMAN' read the following communication : "20, North John-street, Liverpool, 19th March, 1883.— Dear Sir.—Beasiey v. Commissioners,—Our client has pro- mised to see us on Wednesday, and let us know whether be will accept the offer of the Board to split the difference with us as to the mode of taxation of these costs, but he still thinks that the resolution of the Highway and Sanitary Committee recommending that the costs should be taxed upon the . basis of Mr. Russell's letter should be adhered to. If nee- ssarv, the summons against you and the other defendants for contempt in not answering interrogatories can stand over pending our clients decision in order to save expense. We would suggest as the simpler way of carrying out the Board's proposal (in case Mr. Beasley decides to accept it) that the amount taxed off in accordance with the present judgment, should be split, viz., one-half of the total disallowance to be taken off the bill and Mr. Beasley to lose the other half. This would save two separate taxations, one on tho judgment and the other on Mr. Russell's letter.—We are, yours faithfully, JONES and PRIDE. M. Steele, Esq., chairman of Runcorn Com- missioners."—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN wished to know if the Board were comprised in one way or another. (Mr. SHAW: We are not.) Perhaps Mr. Shaw would listen to. what he had got to say; and Mr. Speakman went on to speak of the recommendation of the Sanitary Committee, which Mr. Shaw said was not the business of the Board.—A slight passage at arms between these gentlemen then took Voce, Mr. SPEAKMAN expressing the determination not to be put down by a pri- vate member' and eventually went on to say that there was no doubt about one thing—that the .Board had already in- curred an enormous expense. Where was the matter going to end? What had been put before the "other side" to bring the subject to an issue? Was the Board to go on for everlasting incurring law expenses? were the questions he wished answering.—Mr. SHAW laughingly observed that he thought Mr. Speakman was going to prove something, a re- mark which drew from Mr. Speakman the retort that he might laugh if he liked; it did not make any difference.— The CHAIRMAN intimated that he should reply that the Board would abide by its decision.—Mr. SPEAKMAN wished the recommendation of the Sanitary Committee read, and this having been complied with, the CLERK remarked that it was wit accepted by the Beard. The discussion then ceased.

div.head: AN ANONYMOUS COMMUNICATION.
div.p: AN ANONYMOUS COMMUNICATION.

The CHAIRMAN said he had received an anonymous letter, which be did not intend to read, that brought certain charges against certain parties in the town. He wished to take this opportunity of tell,ng the writer that be should be quite willing. to investigate any charge, but it must be substantiated by the name of the complainant.—Mr. Swenr: The Board would be glad if the writer would meet the Board. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE.

The Highway and Sanitary Committee's minutes con- tained a letter from Mr. C. Wigg acknowledging his appoint- tnent on the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission. He , said the Manchester ship canal, if carried out, to give increased depth of water betweed Liverpool and Runcorn, , with increased facilities for dockage at reasonable -rates, would be of the greatest importance to Runcorn, and he should , give the matter the attention it deserved.— It was resolved that owing to the continued prevalence of scarlatina, the Committee strongly recommend that no child be admitted or re-admitted to school after an attack of such disease without the certificate of a duly qualified medical man, that the child has quite recovered.—The Lords Corn- misaionera of her Majesty's Treasury had sanctioned the appropriation of certain rooms in Waterloo House for the purposes of the Free Public Library.—A. letter WAS read from the Local Government Board directing that Waterloo House I, should be retained by the Commissioners for use as offices and as a Public Library; and it was recommended that Messrs, Shaw, Fisher, and Meadoweroft be appointed a eommittee to piepare an esti- mate of the Cost of fitting up Waterloo House in ac- cordance with the report adopte,i,by the Board on Jan. 17th. DR. STEELE AND THE GAS COMPANY:
EXCITING DISCUSSION: MR. SHAW DEFIES THE
CHAIRMAN.

The CHAIRMAN moved the following resolution, of which he had given notice :—" That a petition be presented by the Rumeorn Improvement Commissioners, conjointly with the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Co. and Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele, of the Old Quay Copper and Alkali Works, Run- corn, to the next court of quarter sessions, holden at Knutsford, praying the court to nominate and appoint seine accountant or other competent person to examine and ascer- tain the actual state and condition present and retrospective of the concern of the Runcorn Gas Coir.pany, in order that the price of gas may be regulated to the consumers in accor- dance with the Act." The Chairman remarked that when this question was before the Board on February 7th, Mr. Whittaker, who was interested in the Gas Company, voted. He did not wish in any way to reflect upon Mr. Whittaker, for whom he had a very great regard and respect, but lie quite believed that at the time Mr. Whittaker voted, lie did not understand that he was disqualified on grounds stated in the 64th section ed the Public Health Act. Part of that section read as follows : " that any member by reason of his being interested in any contract with the Local Board as a shareholder in any joint stock company, be shall not vote at any meeting of the Local Board on any question in which such company are interested, save that in the case of a water company, or other company established for the carrying on of works of a like public nature, this prohibition may be dispensed with by. the Local Government Board." Therefore as Mr. Whittaker was interested in the Gas Company he ought to have got leave to vote.---Mr. SHAW: It is not clear to me, Mr. Chairman.— The CHAIRMAN: Ask the Law Clerk. I have had not only his opinion, but I have taken the opinion of another gentle- man. It is perfectly clear.—Mr. LAKE wished to know if the Chairman meant to say that he would go so far as to refuse to take Mr. Whittaker's vote ?—The CHAIRMAN: Certainly. I wondered at Mr. Whittaker. I thought he would retire. I shall object to his vote certainly. It did not occur to me at the time that he was a shareholder. It will ' be as well to refer the question to the Law Clerk.— Mr. SHAW said the question before the .Board at the meeting referred to bad nothing whatever to do with a contract. If a contract for lighting the streets with gas had been under discussion, then, according to the section quoted no share- holder ought to vote in the matter. But he defied any member to state that they had ever been dealing with a con- tract. They were asking for an auditor to examine the books of the Gas Company, and there was no possible way in which that clause would prevent a person holding shares in the Gas Company from voting. By no means or construction could they twist the clause to say they were dealing with a contract.—The CHAIRMAN said there was no question of com- tract whatever before the Board. Mr. Whittaker was an in- terested party.—M • SHAW stated that the Gas Company was not interested in the inquiry such as the chairman, was ask- ing for at all. What interest had the company in this mat- ter? They were not seeking the inquiry; therefore thiv were not interested in the matter; and on no ground what- ever could the chairman prevent a shareholder from vorill!,. By Act of Parliament interest meant something from which profit was derived; but what profit were the Gas Company

div.head: WARRINGTON CLERGY INSTI-
div.p: THE WARRINGTON CLERGY INSTI-

TUTIONS. The reportslfor the year 1882 of the institution for the relief of the widows and orphans of the clergymen and: of the branch institution at Warrington for the education of the daughters of clergymen are just issued. Of the widows and orphans' fund, the report states that during the past year £2,116 lOs has been distributed in pensions, donations, and bonuses at the rate of 10 per cent, to 19 widows and 5 1 orphans from the diocese of Chester, to 27 widows and 13 orphans from the diocese of Manchester, and to 10 widows and 4 orphans from the diocese of Liverpool. In addition to this grants amounting to £270 have been made for the maintenance and education of 6 pupils (3 from Chester and 3 from Manchester) in the clergy daughters' school, making a total in pensions and dona- tions and grants to the clergy school of £2.686 10s. The committee feel that both the offertories and the sub- scription lists might be very considerably increased. In some districts, where little or nothing was done before, better returns are now made, but they still ask for more offertories and subscriptions. In submitting their report of the clergy daughters' school, the committee are able to give a good account of the general state of the institution. The two vacancies on the Committee caused by the resignation of the fate Lord Egerton of Talton, and of 'Mr. Charles Langton, have been filled up by the appointment of Mr. C. Parr and Dr. Watkins. The treasurer acknowledges a 'grant of £132 8a from the Unappropriated Fund of the Chester Diocesan Finance Association and one of £lOO from the Unappropriated Fund Of the Liverpool Diocesan Finance Association. The anniversary of the institutions for the present year will be held at War- rington, on August 2, the president for the year being Mr. Piers E. Warburton, M.P. The anniversary sermon will be preached in the morning at tlie Parish Church, by Bishop • Kelly.

EASTER EGGS AND THE HARE. do not know whether the weather on Eater Sun- day in your part of the cOuntry was such as to admit of the Newtoni,tn youths of both sexes amusing themselves in the afternoon of that day in the meadows with eggs, the " shells of which hail been dyed by the yellow blossoms of the whin; or whether the pace-eggers had a high old time of it with the masque of "George and the Dragon ;" but it may interest same of your younger readers to know that some time ago the question was raised as to how it came about that, according to South German folk-lore, the chil- dren believe that it is the hare that lays the Easter-eggs. H. Krebs, of Oxford, now gives the following explanation in the Folk-lore Journal: "Originally the hare seems to have been a bird which the ancient Teutonic goddess Ostara (the Anglo-Saxon nitre, or Eostre, as Bede calls her) trans- formed into a quadruped. For this reason the hare, in grate- ful recollection of its former quality as bird and swift mes- senger of the spring goddess, is able to lay eggs on her festival at Easter-time."---I am, sir, dre., Newington, London, S.E. • ANGLO-SCOTUS.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.— MONDAY. CHEAP TELEGRAM. Mr. CHILDERS informed Mr. Puleston that if he would inquire later in the session whe- ther the Government would consider the decision of the House as to cheaper telegrams he would be able to answer him.

REFORMS IN EGYPT.—In reply to Sir H. D. Wolff, Lord S. FITZMAURICE stated that the Government were occupied in carrying out the reforms in Egypt recommended by Lord Dufferin as the circumstances, time, and place would allow. BLOCKING BILLS.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in answer to Mr. Monk, did not think it was desirable to deprive Mr. Warton of the power of blocking bills providing he did not prove absolutely incorrigible. THE KILMAINHAM TRANSACTIOL—The O'DONOGIME called attention to a reported conversation betweed Mr. Parnell and the editor of a Paris newspaper, in which it was alleged that the member for Cork had spoken of himself and his friends as being the arbiters of the situation when released from Kilmainham, and asked, if so, whether that statement did not conflict with the explanation given at the time by the Government, notably by Lord Cerlingford.—Mr. GLAD- STONE said the statement had escaped his attention, but it was wholly inaccurate. The statement made by Lord Carlingford was perfectly true.—Mr. PARNELL asked leave to state that the conversation with him and Mr. O'Kelly re- ported in the newspaper was substantially correct, and Lord Carlingford's statement to the effect that Mr. Parnell took the initiative in the transaction of the "Treaty of Kilmaint ham" was incorrect. COURT OF CRIMINAL APPEAL BILL.—The ATTORNEY- GENERAL moved the second reading of the Court of Criminal Appeal Bill. He said that where small sums of money were concerned there were several courts of appeal, but it seemed anomalous and strange that when the life of a human being was at stake there was no court of appeal whatever. There had been an average of 12,000 convictions Alit indictment during the past year, and it was impossible to say that in some instances an innocent person had not been convicted. Wrong verdicts were often arrived at by juries in civil cases, and no doubt there were many cases in which they had been misdirected by the judge who tried the case. There was no doubt that many grievoue mistakes had been made by juries. If an appeal were given in all cases, he estimated that there ought to be three thousand appeals in a year, and three of them might be heard daily. That would be a great increase of the work of the judges, and therefore he proposed, as an experiment, that an appeal should only be given as a right in capital cases. Of these appeals he thought there would be only a dozen in a year. He had taken every precaution to ensure a speedy decision in cases of appeal, and, with the view of rendering it certain that the decision should be given within the time between sentence and execution, he proposed to extend the time to forty days.— Sir H. GIFFARD said it was possible there might be some few persons unjustly convicted, but 'at present all practical injustice was removed by the jurisdiction exercised by the Home Secretary. It would be equally possible after the passing of the bill that innocent persons should be con- victed. He submitted that the bill was unworkable, and suggested that it was an indirect expedient to get rid of capital punishment. As the bill was wrong in principle it could not be amended in Committee, and he moved its rejection.—The debate was continued by Mr. Waddy, Mr. Grantham, Mr. Hopweod, Mr. O'Donnell, Mr. C. Russell, Sir E. Wilmot, Mr. Serjeant Simon, and Mr. E. Clarke. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The House re-assembled after the Easter recess. The only business done (vas the reading a first time of a consolidated fund bill brought up from the House of Commons. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. NOTICES.—Mr. Hopwood: On that day four weeks to call attention to the Vaccination Laws and move resolutions. THE ALABAMA AWARD.—In reply to Mr. Kennard, Lord E. FITZSIAURICE said the Government had no intention of reopening the question of the Alabama award. RUSSIA AND ARMENIA.—III answer to Mr. McCoan, Mr. GLADSTONE skid his attention had been called to the corres- pondence in the Daily News of Saturday, dated Trebizour, March 18, reprinting the expected imminence of a Russian invasion of Armenia, but her Majesty's Government had received no confirmation of the report. THE CUBAN REFUGEES.—III reply to Sir R. Cross' Mr. GLADSTONE stated that despatches from the Spanish Go- vernment in reference to the Cuban refugees were on their way, and when these were read he should be glad to confer with the right hon. gentleman as to giving facilities for the motion he proposed to move. THE CONGO.—Mr. JACOB BRIGHT called attention to the interests of commerce in South Africa, and moved that no treaty should be made by the Government sanctioning the annexation by any Power of territories on or adjacent to the Congo, or interfering with the freedom hitherto enjoyed in these regions. He said that those well acquainted with Africa averred that there was no treaty in existence by which the Portuguese were entitled to take possession of any part of the country adjacent to the Congo. The Portu- guese in any country did much to make trade impossible, and the cause of this lay principally in the fact that the officials in Portuguese territory were of an ignorant and inferior character, who were badly paid by their Government. By the best authorities the Congo River was decribed as the natural highway to civilisation and nommerce into Africa. He hoped that the Government would not persist in the policy which he feared they were now following. He suggested that there should be an international understanding with reference to the Congo, and he refused to believe that an English Minister would place the gate of Africa in the hands of the one European Power which made bankrupt every country it had entered.—Mr. WHITLEY seconded the motion.—Lord Emmen) FITZMAURICE agreed as to the im- portance of the question. Her Majesty's Government had demanded that the navigation of the Congo, like that of the Danube, should be absolutely free, and they would not 'tolerate the existence of any vexatious tariffs. Her Majesty's Government also reserved whatever engagements were made with native chiefs on the coasts,so that they should not Suffer for anything done by them in the past.— Mr. WODEHOUSE moved an amendment to the effect that any treaty made should afford adequate securities to all the civilising and commercial agencies at work on the Congo.—Mr. GLADSTONE said the Government could not accept the motion, because they could not be shut out entirely from making the best of the situation and endea- vouring to establish some regular government on the Congo. But if they found it expedient to make a treaty, be engaged that it shoulel be made known to Parliament before ratifica- tion, and with an interval of time which would enable Par- liament to express its judgment on it. He hoped that, with that understanding, Mr. Bright would be satisfied.—Mr.. JACOB BRIGHT said that after what the Prime Minister had said he felt compelled to withdraw his resolution.—After some remarks from Sir Stafford Northcote, Sir C. MULE said that the Government had no objection to passing the amendment, which was accordingly agreed to. THE CHINESE OPIUM TRADE.—Sir J. W. PEASE then moved that an address be presented to her Majesty, praying that in all negotiations with China on the subject of the opium duties the Government of China should be treated as an independent State, having full right to arrange its own import duties.—Mr. S. SMITH seconded the motion, which was carried. THE CHANNEL TUNNEL.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN moved the appointment of a committee of five members of the House to join with a committee of the Lords to consider the pro- posed construction of a Channel Tunnel.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE moved an amendment that before entering upon the ques- tion it was desirable to be put in possession of the views of the Government.—Yr. GLADSTONE urged that in a matter of international action there was no course open to the Government but to refer it to Parliament.—Upon a division, Mr. Chamberlain's motion wascarried, and it was agreed to send a message to the House of Lords acquaint- ing them with the resolution. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. Mr. ROIINDELL moved the second reading of the Univer- sities Committee of Privy Council Bill, the object of which is to amend the machinery by which colleges wishing to have changes made in their statutes may seek the interven- tion of the Privy Council.—After some discussion the Bill was withdrawn.—Mr. REID moved the second reading of the Vivisection Abolition Bill.—A long discussion followed, and Sir Joseph M‘Kenna was speaking when by the rules of the House the debate stood adjourned. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. The Government Bill for the amendment of the MeOlcal Act was introduced by Lord Carlingford. The bill makes very important changes in the existing law with regard to the registration of medical men. It purposes to establish district boards, to which extensive powers as to the training and registration of medical men should be entrusted. The bill was read a second time after considerable discussion. GrOMMONS T HOUSE _ __ 6F HIIRSDAY. THE 'BUDGET: REMISSION OF TAXATION; The Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. CHILDERS, made his first Budget statement. Dealing with the revenue of the past year, the right hon. gentleman said the total amount received had been £89,004,000, which exceeded the original estimate by £4,069,000, the July estimate by £1,500,000, and the highest estimate he had formed, in February, by £750,000. The receipts under Excise and Customs had been £46,587,000 for 1881-2, and the estimate for 1882-3 and the receipts for 1882-3 had been almost the same. He drew attention to the present consumption of spirits and wine in this country, remarkipg that a e spirit duty in 1875-6 amounted to £23,000,000, and that if the consumption had proceeded at the same rate the duty last year, allowing for the increase of population, would have amounted to £24,840,000. whereas it was only £19,840,000. The revenue from beer had been £8,380,000, which was under the tathnate. The falling off he attributed to the hop famine. The actual expenditure was £88,906,000, and compared with the revenue of £89,004,000 this gave a surplus on the laccount for 1882-3 of just £98,000.
