div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY APRIL 7, 1883. DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY APRIL 7, 1883. DISTRICT NEWS.

war expenditure on account of the operations in South Africa, in Afghanistan, and in the Transvaal. They had to pay out of taxation altogether on account of war expenditure £10,700,000, and they left no arrears on account i f the wars in which they had been engaged. Passing to the year 1883-4, the estimated expenditure w.is £85.789.000, or less than the ex- penditure of lasc year by £3,117,000. With regard to the operations for reducing the National 'Debt, since 1857 the amount of the reduction of the debt had been £107,100,000, and the further reduction owing to the operations he con- templated was such that after twenty years the debt would hays been reduced by £172,000,000, and the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer would have at his disposal £3,374,000 a year of annuities falling in for use either in relief of taxation or otherwise. The estimate for the present year, considering the state of trade and agricalture was a safe but not a sanguine estimate. The total taxed revenue was estimated at £73,385,000, and the non-taxed revenue £15,095,000, be- ing a total of £88,480,000; as ageing a ttxed revenue last year of £73,128, 000,and a non-taxed revenue of £15,876,000, being a total of £89,004,000. There would thus be a sur- plus of £2,091,000. - Ho proposed to make some slight alterations in the mode of collecting the income tax, and to issue occasional game gun licencea lasting fourteen days. The Government proposed to allow silver, whether manufactured or imported, to be deposited in bond in a species of warehouse where it would be open to inspection by the public, it only plying the duty when sold or removed. He proposed ultimately to repeal the tax altogether. It would absorb about £lO,OOO this year. He had set aside £f70,000 to give effect to the resolution of the House in regard to cheap telegrams. A further reduction would be made in the passenger duty, which would be taken off all fares of a penny per mile and under, involving a loss of about £400,000, and dating from October 1 next. These reductions left a balance of £2,375,000, and out of that he proposed to take 1p off the income tax. That would cost £2,135,000, and leave a final balance of £240. Sir S. NcomicarE was glad to find that the condition of the country was , not so bad as there had been reason to apprehend, and I complained that the Chancellor of the Exchequer had made \ , one of the most controversial and partisan speeches that he had ever listened to on a Budget night. —The debate was continued by Sir W. J. Pease, Sir H. Peek Mr. Monk, Mr. Salt, Mr. Dodds, Alderman Lawrence, Mr. Illingworth, Mr. Sexton, Mr. Labouchere, Sir G. campbell, Mr. Arnold, Mr. Biddell, Mr. O'Brien, Mr. F. Buxton, Sir J. Lubbock, and Mr. T. P. O'Connor.—Mr. CHILDERS haying replied, the resolution confirming the reduction of the income tax was passed, and progress was reported.
THE FENIAN CONSPIRACY.
ASHTON.

THE SERIOUS JEWELLERY ROBBERY AT ASHTON.—At the Wigan County Poiice Court on Friday last, Thomas Varty Whelley, was charged on remand with stealing two gold brooches, seven pairs of gold ear-rings, two gold wedding rings, two silver chains, two silver breastpins, one silver case, one silver bracelet, one spying watch key, three silver necklets, one silver lever watch, and two morofflo cases from a shop at,Ashton, and Elizabeth Sherrington and Lucy Sherrington, Barton-terrace, Wigan, were charged with receiving the same knowing them to be stolen.' There was a further charge preferrea against the prisoners of steal- ing and receiving five'goll rings, three pairs of goll ear- rings, one pair of silver ear-rings, and one overcoat from the same place.—Mr. Parkerson defended the female prisoners. The value of the property was stated to be £22. The facts have already appeared in these columns.—Prisoners were committed to the sessions for trial. HAYDOCK.

The annual re-election of three members of the Haydock Local Board has again passed off without a contest. The only persons nominated were the three retiring members, Mr. Wm. Balh.rry, farmer, Ashton-road ; Mr. Jno. Cunliffe, licensed victualler, Blackbrook ; and Mr. John Greenhall, gentleman, Clipsley-lane, and accordingly under the pro- visions of the&ublic Health Act, 1875, they have been de- clared by Mr. -John Jackson, deputy returning officer, to be duly elected.

SPECIAL MEETING OF THE HAYDOCK LOCAL BOATID. A special meeting of the members of the Haydock Local • Board, for the Purpose of making a general district rate for the ensuing year and for the purpose of considering the an- nual report of the medical officer of health (Dr. Watkins), was held at the Local Board Offices, on Monday afternoon last. The members present were Charles Pilkington, Esq., J.P. (in the chair), Mr. John Jackson, and Mr. Cook.—Mr. Jackson moved that a gent district rate of 101 in the .2 be made for the purpose of defraying the expenses incurred by the Haydock Local Bowl in the execution of the Public 1 Health Act, 1875.—Mr. Cook seconded the motion, and it I was carried.—Owing to the small attendance of members the , consideration of the medical officer's report was deferred, and I the meeting concluded.

JUDICIA/: SEPAUATION.—Matthew Littler, Haydock, was charged at Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednes- day with having assaulted his wife Harriet.—Complainant said she and her husband were at St. Helens on Saturday, the 24th February. Her husband caljed at several places, and she had to wait for him. They went into a friend's house and stayed there a while, but she wanted to catch the eight o'clock train for home, and as her husband would not go she went out of the house by herself. Her husband fol- lowed immediately afterwards, struck her, knocked her down, and stamped on her face with his foot. He had abused her before, and this was the fourth time she bad had to leave him. She wanted a separation, for she had tried him as long as she could.—The defendant was committed to prison for three months, and a judicial separation was granted, the prisoner being ordered to pay 12s. per week towards the maintenance of his wife and family. BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT HAYDOCK.—On Satur- day, John Heaton was charged, at Newton Petty Sessions, with having assaulted his wife, Nancy Heaton.—The prose- cutrix stated that she and her husband went home together about half-past one on Monday morning, and when they had been in the house a short time a quarrel arose between them. Her husband hit her and kicked her on the body a great number of times, knocked her down several times, and pulled a quantity of hair from her head, and said be would kill her. The prosecutrix showed the Bench a quantity of hair (which she said had been pulled from her head by the defendant) as well as a number of black marks on her arms and neck. On her face were also a number of black marks and bruises.—The defendant admitted haying struck his wife and knocked her down, but sajd he would not have done so had he not received intense provocation. She got the poker up to strike him, and said she would make him ass wit her. He wanted to be separated.—The Bench con- sidered this a very brutal case, and fined defendant 40s. and costs.

HUYTON-WITH-ROBY. IMPUDENT GAME TRESPASS AT ROBY. A smartly. dressed young man named John Baker, was summoned be- fore the Prescot magistrater(Mr. Evans and Mr. Willis), on Tuesday, for trespassing in pursuit of ganie on land at Roby, in the occupation of Mr. Gore Ashton. Seymour Lonsdale was summoned for participating in the same offence, but did not appear, and Mr. J. 0. Swift, who prosecuted on behalf of Mr. Ralph Brocklebank, of Childwall Hall, who preserves the game on Mr. Ashton's land, obtained permission to with- draw the summons against Lonsdale.—lt was stated that Lonsdale and a young man named Anderson, applied to Mr Brocklebank to try a greyhound with a course or two over his land, but Ile refused. After that defendant Baker told them he had liberty to go over the land, and persuaded them to take the dog out. They started from Childwall Hall and from there went to Roby, where John Harrison, a teamsman, employed by Mr. Erle of Roby, saw the dog come out of Mr. Pennington's field, get a hare out of Mr. Erie's field, and course it into Mr. Ashton's field, where it turned it four times. Defendants Anderson and Lonsdale followed the dog after that across Mr. Erie's park, down Cair's-lane, and into Mr. Pilkington's park. Altogether Harrison saw three dis- tinct courses, the last of which finished on Mr. Pilkington's lawn. The defendant, with his companions, also called at the Stanley Arms, Roby, where he said ho was Mr. Brockle- bank, but they would not know him as he had not got his leggings on.—The Chairman (Mr. W. L. Evans) said defen- dant had committed a very impudent offence in fact, a great many offences, and he had also incited two other young men to break the law. The Bench, therefore, inflicted the full penalty of 40s, and costsl3s.

Superior, on the 11th February. Mr. Marshall prosecuted, and said that the prisoner had been convicted 23 times as being a rogue and vagabond. The prisoner was a person apparently _unable or unwilling to work, and went about farms, !guns, and outhouses and slept amongst straw' and hay, and'he had been found in such a position as to cause terror to the farmers.—PS. Gunn proved a previons con- viction against the prisoner.—P.C. Riddlesworth deposed to finding the prisoner asleep under some hay on a farm, and on bringing him into the police station he found upon him a box of matches, some tobacco and a pipe.—Prisoner: What are you? Do you ever read your Bible; do you ever say your prayers? • • (Laughter.) Do you say you. found some tobacco and a pipe upon me ?—Witness: Yes.— Prisoner: What is your name; 'where do you come from? (Laughter.)—The Deputy-Chairman: His name is William Riddlesworth.--Prisoner : Is that statement true P—Riddles- worth : It is perfectly true.—Prisoner: Is them words true ? (No reply) Who anthorised *you to apprehend me ?—The Deputy-Chairman: Why, the law authorised him. I don't think he is bound to answer that question to you.-Prisoner: Well, I say if you will acquit me I will go to the Work- house. an I promise you I will not come here again.—The Deputy-Chairman said if the prisoner could not take care of himself he must be taken care of. Prisoner was sen- tenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour.

div.head: DISCOVERY OF EXPLOSIVES IN LONDON AND
div.p: DISCOVERY OF EXPLOSIVES IN LONDON AND
BIRMINGHAM.

On Thursday morning the Birmingham police made an important seizure of explosives, and unearthed what may prove to be a conspiracy connected with the recent Fenian attempts to destroy public buildings. About two months ago, a respectably-dressed young man, giving the name of A. G. Whitehead, took a shop in Ledsam-street, near the Mount Pleasant public-house and started ostensibly as a paperhanger and oil seller. Ile took lodgings next door, at the house of a Mrs. Pointon, where be had his meals and slept, and conducted himself, as his landlady says, "in quiet and gentlemanly manner." According to the testi- mony of persons living in the locality', he does not seem to I have disposed of more than a few shillings' worth of stock ' during the time he has occupied the shop. What at last attracted suspicion was the fact that large consignments of chemicals—which/could be of no possible use in the paper- hanging trade—reached the shop from time to time, and were a:owed away out of sight. The premises, it should be explained, consist of a front shop, a back room, and a small kitchen. These consignments of chemicals were put away in the back compartments. Within the last few days, information has reached the police which led to the place being-closely watched. On Thursday morning, about seven o'clock, two detectives paid a sudden visit to his lodgings next door, and the landlady came downstairs I immediately. Whitehead got up at once, and on going out into the street was arrested by the officers. An examination of the premises was then made, resulting in some very sus- picious revelations. The front shop contained a paltry stock of wall paper and several cans of oil, mostly common oil, but two cans of glycerine. In the back room there were I eleven great jars of chemicals and a number of cans: In the' back kitchen things bore a still more suspicious aspect. The ordinary washing furnace was filled with a liquid preparation, and to carry away the fumes a line had been made connecting it with the chimney. The furnace contained several gallons of this mysterious compound. Near the furnace were lying a thermometer and other chemical apparatus. The kitchen smelled strongly of the previous night's operations. There were several jars of oil and acid in the kitchen, two being labelled sulphuric acid. The place was at once taken pos- session of by the police, and the strictest secrecy was observed, very few of the residents in the neighbourhood knowing anything about the seizure till the most ex- travagant rumours got in circulation two or three hours afterwards. The police ransacked the place in the hope of finding some documents which would throw light upon Whitehead's operations, but as far as we can learn they were unsuccessful. Whitehead seems to have done his work with remarkable circumspection. No one in the neighbourhood had the slightest suspicion of him, and only on one occasion Ras any smell perceived from the premises. This was some days ago, when Mrs. Pointon perceived a strong smell from the direction of Whitehead's kitchen, and when she remarked upon it to him he replied that he was only boiling some oils. Whitehead, is described as being a short, , dark young man, of gentlemanly appearance, and of exceed- ingly quiet demeanour. Although be spent most of his evenings at home' he rarely conversed with his landlord or landlady, though he occasionally took some notice of the children. It is supposed by the police that the paperhanging business was simply "a blind" to conceal the operations at the back of the premises. Dr. Hill was sent for, and he im- mediately took some samples of the chemicals for analysis. The police are hopeful before long of tracing tho prisoner's dealings with other men in different parts of the country, but any speculations on that point cannot be safely made until the police have time to prosecute their inquiries further.

In connection with the discovery at Birmingham' import- ant arrests have been made in London, where also large quantities of dynamite have been discovered. On Wednes- day morning an elderly man engaged rooms at a private hotel in Southampton-street, Strand, for a Mr. Norman, who was described as a medical student, and in due course the young gentleman arrived with a heavy box, which was Car- ried upstairs by a man who accompanied him. A few hours afterwards—shortly after midnight—four detectives arrived, arrested Mr. Norman, and took possession of his box, which was found to contain nearly 2 cwt, of pure nitro-glycerine. It is remarked as singular that the hotel at which the arrest was made is the property of the editor of the Court Circular, whose office is in the lower part of the building, and who has recently received threatening letters. Later in the day a second man, who had been seen with Norman, was arrested, and he also had a large quantity of sitio-glycerine in his possession, and at the same time a third mon who was in company with the second prisoner was arrested. One of these men, calling himself Wilson, has been living about a week at Nelson-square, Blackfriars, where the secrecy of his movements excited suspicion._ On Wednesday he said he was going to Wolverhampton, and took with him a black bag. He returned on Thursday, ac- companied by his fellow prisoner, and found five detectives awaiting his arrival. The police succeeded in making another arrest on Thursday evening, but are very reticent on the subject. More arrests are expected. There appears to be ground for hoping that the dynamite conspiracy may be broken.

div.head: STATEMENT BY THE. HOME SECRETARY.
div.p: STATEMENT BY THE. HOME SECRETARY.

In the House of Commons on Thursday evening, a question was put by Sir S. Northcote as to the seizure of explosives in London, to which Sir W. Hatcourt replied that at an early hour in the morning a man had been arrested with a box containing newt. of liquid in an india-rubber bag. This bad been examined at Woolwich, and was found to be a highly explosive compound, believed to be nitro- glycerine. The man came from Birmingham, where there had been -discovered a manufactory on a large scale appar- ently of explosive material. A second arrest had been made that afternoon of a person who had been seen in the com- pany of the other man, and he bad a large quantity of material apparently of the s Imo character. In the company of this second nian was a third with a large sum of money upon him, a considerable portion of which was in American notes. There were three men in custody in London and one .in Birmingham in connection with this manufactory of explosives. The right honourable gentleman added that he was not at all satisfied with the existing state of the law on 1 this subject, which in his opinion required a very early amendment.

VOLUNTEER CONCERT AT ST. HELENS.—OR Monday evening a concert was given in the Volunteer Hall, St. Helens, under the patronage of his Worship the Mayor and other officers of the 21st L.R. Volunteers, in aid of the widow and children of the late Sergeant-Instructor R. Cub- bin. There was a large and appreciative audience present, and the miscellaneous programme submitted was a most excellent one, containing as it did contributions by most of the better known local vocalists and instrumentalists, all of whpm rendered their services gratuitously. Musical selections were also skilfully discoursed by the St. Helens and Prescot bands of the regiment, the former under the conductorship of Mr. George Parr, and the latter of Mr. W. Arkell. The opening song" Arm, arm, ye brave," was ex- cellently sung by Mr. Merrill, after whom Miss Swift won an encore by her " Ehren on the Rhine." The Misses Bar- foot next gave an admirable duet on the pianoforte, and Miss Parry, whose songs are so generally and so deservedly appreciated, won an enthusiastic recall by her " Winter's story." Mr. I'. Massey's skilful handling of the violin was properly rewaided by an encore, as was also a humorous , song "The Waterford boys," by Mr. Banks The song "The gilasy girl" was finely rendered by Miss Farran, and Mr. George Barton sang a ballad "Farewell my mountain home" with all his usual success. in the second part Miss Parry was very successful in rendering the beautifully pathetic song "Home they brought her warrior dead ;" as 1 was also Mr. George Barton with his song "0. give me - back my Arab steed." A zither solo by Miss Barfoot won a deserved encore, and fora really Magnificent performance on the concertina Mr. Charsley was similarly rewarded. Mr. G. L. Coombs, it must also be added, largely contributed to the pleasure of the evening by his contribution, which showed him to be a comic singer of more than usual versa- tility.

div.head: IRLAM.
div.p: IRLAM.

TOWNSHIP MEETING.—The annual ratepayers' meeting for the purpose of appointing overseers for the township of Irlam was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Liverpool-road, Irlam, on Monday evening. Mr. H. Goodier presided, and there was a small attendance.—Mr. Speers stated that the total highway rate amounted to £Bl Ss. 71A., and the total, collected was £7B 15s. 4d.; arrears (recoverable), £2 2s. Id. There was a balance in hand of £2O 19s. 9d. The total expenditure was aq 17s. 4d., leaving a balance in hand of £32 16s. 9d.—Mr. J. Hesford proposed, and Mr. J. Skarp seconded, the passing of the accounts, which was carried.— Mr. Speers stated that the Salford Corporation had refused to pay for repairs which had been made on the highway on their behalf. It was resolved " that a letter be written to the gas engineer notifying that the authority of the surveyor will in future have to be obtained befern the servants of the Corporation take up the footpaths in the hamlet."—A short discussion with reference to the tollbar took place, and it was resolved "that the chairman be instructed to seek the advice of Messrs. taylor, kirkman, and Colley, on behalf of the ratepayers, respecting the recovery of Government land from the county."—Messrs. G. and J. Hoyle were ap- pointed surveyors for the ensuing year.

div.head: KNOWStiY.
div.p: KNOWStiY.

RETIREMENT OF P.C. WADDINGTON.—P.C. Waddington who has been stationed at Knowsley for the last nineteen years, having completed a service of twenty-five years in the police force has retired upon a pension of 25 6d per day. Mr. Waddington joined the Prescot division in 1855, and did duty at Prescot for six years, during which time as well as during his long sojourn at Knowsley, he earned and sustair.ed a reputation for straightforwardness and honesty.

div.head: LOWTON.
div.p: LOWTON.

TOWNSTLIPannuaI meeting of ratepayers of the township of Lowton was held in St. Luke's Boys' Schoolroom on Thursday evening. The rector, the Rev. R. Smith, presided, ani there was only a poor attendance. Mr. Mather having read the notice convening the meeting, the overseers' accounts were then submitted, which showed the total expenditure to be £ll4 3s 11d, and t'ao balance in hand £164 13s.—Mr. Arnott proposed that the accounts be passed. —Mr. Unsworth seconded the motion which was adopted.— Messrs. John Bent, J. Laycock, and john Wood were nomi• nated as overseers.—:Mr. Arnott proposed the re-election of Mr. S. Bent as waywarden. He bad done the work well.— Mr. Joseph Mort seconded the motion, which was carried.— Mr. Mather reported that Mr. Penkethman wished to resign. —Mr. Mort: I propose Mr. Arnott.—Mr. Laycock seconded. —The Chairman pointed out that the election was for three years now.—fr. Arnott proposed Mr. Guest —Mr. 'John Bent seconded.—Messrs. Arnottand Guest were duly elected. Upon the suggestion of the Chairman, Messrs. Eckersley, Unsworth, and John Bent were unanimously recammended to the commissioners as assessors of taxes.—Mr. Mather sub- mitted the report of the County Rate ,Committee, which axed the gross estimated rateable value of Lowton at £19,370 7s and the nett at £8,933 ss.—The other business was of a routine charactet.

LYMM. LOCAL BOAIID ELECTION.—This week the ratepayers of LyMm have undergone the excitement attendant on the election of members of the Local Board. The candidates were Hugh Cameron, Lymm, land agent; George Hall, Oak I Lea, Lymm, gentleman; Daniel Rogers, Statham commis- sion agelit ; John Thomason, Bridgewater-street, shoe manu- facturer; and Thomas Woolley, Mill-lane, gentleman. The voting papers were collected yesterday, and Mr. Callender, the returning-officer, is expected to announce the result at noon to-day (Saturday). div.head: RAINFORD.
div.p: RAINFORD.

LOCAL BOARD ELECTION —There will be no contest this year in connection with the election of five members for the Rainford Local Board, as only five persons have been nomi- nated. These are Messrs. James Agnew, Thomas Kerfoot, John Whalley, Richard Webster, all of whom are retiring members; and Mr. Gilbert Brown in place of Mr. John Birchall .

ALLEGED THEFT OF OATS AT RAINFORD.—On -Monday, at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, a respectable-looking man, named Richard Wilkinson, was charged with having stolen a quantity of oats, valued at 6s. Bd., the property of Thomas Boardman, farmer, at Rainford, on the 24th ult. It appeared that the defendant had been employed by Board- man, and on the 23rd ult. had been told by him to take the cart out on the following morning, but not to take any corn with him for the horse. On the following morning, how- ever, prosecutor met him, and looking into the cart, found the oats in a bag. Defendant denied knowing that the oats had been in the cart, and as there was insufficient evidence to support the charge It was dismissed.

div.head: RIXTON.
div.p: RIXTON.

RIDING ON THE CHESHIRE LINES COMMITTEE'S RAIL- WAY WITHOUT A TICKET. Mary Travis, wife of George Travis, Rixton-with-Glazebrook, was on Wednesday charged at Warrington County Petty Sessions with having ridden from Warrington to Glazebrook on the Cheshire Lines Rail- way without a ticket on the 15th February. Defendant rode from Warrington to Glazebrook by the train which ar- rives at the latter place about nine o'clock in the evening, but when asked for her ticket she said she had got a return ticket, and had lost the return half. The booking clerk ex- amined his book and found that no return ticket had been issued that day, and he remembered the defendant taking a single fare ticket for Warrington in the morning.—The de- fendant was fined 10s. and costs, in all £1 is. ed. TRESPASSING IN PURSUIT OF GAME AT WOOLSTON.—Jas. Harrison and Nathan Harrison, Rixton, were charged at Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, with havieg trespassed in pursuit of game on land in the occupa- tion of the Cheshire Lines Committee, at Woolstbn.—Chas. Monk, gamekeeper to Mr. James Reynolds, said that a num- ber of wires were set on the land on the 28th ult., and he watched the place on the following day. About noon he saw the two defendants go on to the land. Nathan Harrison picked up a rabbit from one of the wires, and the other defendant was coming in the direction of another wire, when he espied witness, and ran into a cabin close by. Witness followed and asked him for the rabbit, and he replied that he had not got one, but witness went into the cabin and found it on the floor.—Nathan Harrison said they were both working on the Cheshire Lines planting trees, and he did not go on the land in pursuit of game, but far another purpose. He was above two.bundred yards from the other defendant. —James Harrison, who admitted having taken up the rab- bit, was fined 10s. and costs, and the summons against Nathan was dismissed.

div.head: WHISTON.
div.p: WHISTON.

DEATH FROM MIENS AT WHISTON WORICHOITSE.—An inquest was held at the workhouse, Whiston, on Tuesday, on the body of a woman, 83 years ef age, named Elizabeth Dixon. Deceased formerly lived at Giller's-green, Eccles- ton, where on the 4th ult, she accidentally fell against a fireplace and was burned. She was removed to the work- house hospital and seemed to rally, and her wounds to heal, but on Saturday morning she died somewhat suddenly. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

AN UNGRATEFUL PROTEGE AT WITISTON.—A boy, 15 years of age, named Joseph Firth. was charged at Prescot on Tuesday with stealing a collier's lamp and a pair of boots, value 9s, the property of William Kay, collier, Lane-ends, Whiston. On the 24th February the prisoner went to Kay's house, and representing that be was destitute, said he would work for him if Kay would take him in. Accordingly Kay gave him shelter and took him to work with him in a coal mine, but on the 13th March he disappeared with a pair of boots and a lamp.—Superintendent Barker stated that after leaving Whiston the prisonee went to Liverpool and pawned the boots in Sawney Pope-street. From thence he rambled to Ormskirk, where he pawned the lamp. If he had stopped with Kay he might have had a good home, and become a respectable member of society.--Prisoner said his mother was living, but he did not know where she was. He had been in Marsh-lane Industrial School, Liverpool —Kay said prisoner told him that Joseph Firth, farmer, Whiston, was hie. cousin, and he ascertained from Mr. Firth that such was the case. The prisoner also told him he had an uncle at Rainhill, and it was partly on these representations that he took him in.—P,risoner was sentenced to 14 days' imprison- ment.

div.head: WINSFORR
div.p: WINSFORR

PRIMMVE MgruordsTs.—The annual gathering of the Sunday school, Station-road Methodists took place on Sun- day. This "sitting up" and sermons for the benefit of the school funds is thought much of, and the friends of the school come from fiar and near to hear how the children sing and say pieces, &c., as much as to bear the preacher. They had the Rev. W. Turner from Stafford Sunday last, afternoon and night, when good sermons, nice singing, and pretty children doing their best, met their reward from ad- miring parents, friends, and neighbours. FREE METHODISTS.—A series of special services are being held in High-street chapel during this and following weeks. The circuit has had the benefit of Miss Mctiatchie's services at Holmes chapel last week, and Winsford is reaping the harvest, if such it may prove, Sunday, Tuesday, and Wed- nesday. etc., the large chapel has been well attended. Her discourses have been "Two blind men," "Descent of the Holy Ghost at Pentecost," etc., the Rev. W. T. Symons pre- ailed on Sunday for her, other friends taking the lead each other night.

div.head: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.
div.p: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

The Council of the West Cheghire Liberal Association have unanimously selected Mr. David Duncan, of Gayton Hall, Neston, a Liverpool merchant, 'to contest West Cheshire at the next election in conjunction with Mr. James Tomkinson.

THE CHAAIRMANSHIP OF CHESTER QUARTER SESSIONS.— At the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace for the County of Chester, held at Knutsford, on Monday, Lord Eaerton of Teton was unanimously elected chairman in succession to his late father. A resolution expressing the high and grateful sense which the court entertained of the services rendered by the late Lord Egerton as lord lieuten- ant and as chairman of the Quarter Sessions Was also adopted, on the motion of the Duke of Westminster, who has received the appointment of Lord Lieutenant of the county in succession to the deceased nobleman. CREWE CATTLE MARKET AND ABATTOIRS COMPANY.— The second annual meeting of the shareholders was held at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, on Saturday afternoon; Col. Buller, V.C., presiding. Among others present were the Duke of Sunderland, Sir Henry Green, and General Sir Arnold Kimball. The report, which was moved by the chairman, dealt with the progress of the new buildings, which are being erected at a cost of nearly £12,000, and ex- pressed thee hope that theyswould be completed by the first .week in June, when the shareholders would possess a market equal to any in the kingdom. The report was adopted, and Dr. Atkinson, one of the retiring directors, was re-elected.— The Duke of Sunderland proposed that the directors of the company should be found £5O a year each for their servicea until the undertaking pays 5 per cent, the question of their remuneration to be then re-considered. This was agreed to. CHESHIRE CONGREGATIONAL Umorr.—The annual meet? ing of the Cheshire Congregational Union was held on Wednesday, at Bowdon, Mr. B. S. Bostock presiding. The Chairman in his address directed attention to the excellent results of voluntaryism as exemplified in the Congrega- tionalist denomination, and suggested improvements which might be made in their organisation with a view to their making more rapid progress. A resolution was adopted in favour of the preaching of simultaneous temperance ser- mons throughout the Union, and a discussion took place on the training and supply of young men for the ministry, ending in the passing of a resolution instructing the Executive Committee to consider and bring up a scheme by means of which the interests of the colleges of the denomi- nation and the importance of supplying ministers to meet the needs of the churches might be periodically brought before the Union.
" LIFTING " IN CHESHIRE : ATTEMPT TO REVIVE AN OLD, CT:STOIC—A case illustrating the remarkable survival
I WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS

The last meeting of this Board was held at the Work- house on Wednesday. Present—Mr. G. Blackhurst (ehair- man), Rev. G. F. Robertm, Messrs. Brown, Longshaw, Burn, Appleton, Greening, Cartwright, Humphries, Hunt, Green- all, Marsh, Bonnell, Gibson, Darbyshire' Cooper, Woo!fall, Taylor, Houghton, Caldwell, Garnett,Yonge, Hall, and Sutton (clerk). •

THE NEW SCHOOLS. The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board, dated 21st March, acknowledging receipt of a letter enclosing the certificate by the architect/ of the new schools for the Union, that the schools had been erected in accord- ance with the approved plans and also a certificate by the medical officer that the schools were fit for occupation. The writer was directed -to state that looking to the certificate of the medical officer the Board saw no objection to the schools being occupied by the children.

REMOVAL AND DESERTION CASES. Major CARTWRIGHT stated that there was no case for removal, and no able-bodied in the house. The officials within the past few months had taken a cou#Se both with regard to the apprehension and conviction of people whose families were chargeable to the Union which had put the Union in a more favourable position in regard to desertion than they had been since he was a member of the Board.— Mr. APPLETON: Can you tell us bow many desertions there are P—Major CARTWRIGHT : A great many. I believe wa we have in the house 130 or 140 children. Mr. Aprz.rrow: Here P—Major CARTWRIGHT : Yes. That was in addition to the number of children at the Barracks. Unless they adopted the boarding-out system very shortly there would be no room for the children. The Board only had room for 200 children, and he was very glad they were bound to make provision for children, as it was far less ex- pensive to board them out, and thatibad been found out by Unions which had erected palatial buildings such as they had.

SUNDAY CLOSING OF PUBLIC HOUSES. The CLERK read a petition he had received in favour of closing public-houses on Sunday for adoption by the Board. —Mr. DARBYSHIRE moved, and Mr. BURN seconded, that petition be adopted, and dwelt upon the advantages that would be derived from the Sunday closing of public-houses. —Mr. TAYLOR, as chairman of the local Licensed Victuallers' Association, stated that it had been clearly proved that there was less drunkenness on Sunday than on any other day, and he therefore did not see why the chairman should sign the petition.—Mr. GREENING supported the motion, remarking that the sooner public-houses were closed the better it would be for the whole community.—Major CARTWRIGHT : Altogether? (Cries of "Yes.")—Mr. GREENING did not mean to say that public-houses should be closed altogether, but on Sunday; although it would not take much to convince him of the desirability of closing them altogether. (Laughter.)—Mr. COOPER stated that there was a resolution on the books which said that no petition should be signed unless due notice had been given to the members, and he thought it was only fair that the members should exercise their dis- cretion.—Major CARTWRIGHT could not help admiring the interest several members of the Board took in suppressing the drink traffic. They could not blame them. But he had no doubt there was a number of very respectable people connected with the business who would only be too glad if there was a general closing of public-houses on Sunday. His impression was that time would bring about the change desired.—The CLERK explained that the resolution referred to by Mr. Cooper was only applicable to the year in which it was passed.—Mr. COOPER then moved an amendment, that the matter be adjourned until that day fortnight so that notice could be sent to each member.—Me. HUMPHRIES seconded the amendment, and on a vote being taken there were 7 for the amendment and 16 for the motion, which was carried.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. Mr. DARBYSHIRE, on the minutes of the School Fees Committee coming up for confirmation, said, that during the year there had been 574 appli- cations for fees, which were granted in 478 cases. The number of children for whom fees were allowed was 1,005, so that the Board would see that the committee had had a good deal to do during the year. He added that the committee had been attended exceedingly well.—Mr. GARNETT thought the fees should be granted on condition that so many attendances should be made each week. He thought that would have .a good effect, for he believed there was a good deal of carelessness in respect to the attendances of children for whom school fees were allowed.—Mr. DARRYsHmEremarli there had not been many cases of the kind Mr. Garnett bad alluded to, and he thought in the future the committee and the attendance officers would do their best to obtain regular attendance.— The CHAIRMAN thought the thanks of the Board were due to the committee for the great care they bad taken. in regard to these cases.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: VOTES OF THANKS.
div.p: VOTES OF THANKS.

Mr. DausystunE proposed a vote of thanks tO the chair- man for presiding over the Board during the year. He was sure they would all agree with him Mr. Blackhurst had per- formed that duty to the satisfaction of all the members of the Board. There might have been trying times, but the chairman had always risen with the occasion, and he thought Mr. Blackhurst had performed the duties of chairman in an important and business-like manner. He thought the thanks of the Board were due to the chairman for doing 80, and also for his regular attendance.—The Rev, J. YONGE seconded the proposition. He supposed by some people the position of chairman of the Board of Guardians was looked upon with considerable envy. Whether the position of chairman of the Board of Guardians of the Warrington Union was a position to be envied be left them to jud2e. (Hear, bear.) At any rate, whatever'was the character of it in past history, he thought Mr. Blackburst was fully entitled to their cordial thanks for the way in which he had discharged the duty for the past 12 months. His own opinion was the chairman had grappled with the difficulties presented to the Board in a very fair and very satisfactory manner; and he should like to take the opportunity of saying—which he did with a good deal of earnestness—he did not sympathise at all with that unfortunate article which appeared in The Examiner a fort- night ago, in reference to the proceedings of that Board. He thought the way in which that paper thought fit to reflect on the chairman very ill became the organ of the Liberal party, and very ill became any paper in the town that affected to know anything of what took place at that Baud. He thought Mr. Blackhurst had Ilene the,best hecould under the circumstances in which be had been placed. Unfortun- ately some members had a marvellous tendency to talk; so much 90 that he thought they might be even called obstruc- tionists—(bear, hear)—and he •hoped the ratepayers in the discharge of their duty, which they would be called upon to discharge in the next few days, would endeavour to return such men as with their talk would combine wisdom, and enable the Board to have a happier history in the future than it had been in the past.—Messrs. LONGSHAW, GREENING, BURN, APPLETON, and HALL sup- ported the proposition, which was carried unanimously.— :The CHAIRMAN severally thanked the members for the very flattering manner in which they had spoken of him. He certainly did net expect it when he came into the room. It was true in the last twelve months they had passed through tempestuous times, but they had agreed to differ many times, and he could only say that he bad always qndeavoured to act impartially and to obtain for everyone a fair hearing. He had been blamed in the paper for not lacing a little more stern with the members, and he might perhaps have been to blame on that occasion. However' be should, notwithstanding the little squabbles they had had during the year, look back upon the year he had served as chairman of that Board with pleasure. (Hear, hear.) He complained that he had not had quite that support from members he had a right to expect, but they would let by-gones be by-gones and in future try to be a little more harmonious and charitable one to the other. -Then he thought they would get on a deal better and do more for the interests of those they repesented. Thanks were also given to the vice- chairmen and to Messrs. Woolfall, Yonge, and Hall, who decline to serve again as guardians. The proeeedings then terminated.

div.head: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD,
div.p: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD,
A meeting of this board was held in the Sessions'House, Daresbury, on Thursday. Mr. Edward Greenall presided, and a large number of members were present.
PRESTON BROOK BRIDGE,

The CLERK read a letter from the Bridgewater Navigation Co., which stated that the company's engineer had examined this bridge, and had reported that there was no fear for the safety of the bridge, and that the water dripping through was not from the canal, but was the rain from the bank, and was less than at any previous time. The company promised to have the wall cemented.—A letter was also read from Mr. J. W. Arthur, drawing attention to the unsafe state of the road from Soot Hill bottom to Pennington Bridge, but the CHAIRM&N said that the road was repairable by the River Weaver Trust, and the Clerk read an agreement of 1876, showing that the River Weaver Trustees undertook the re- pair of the road.—The Clerk was therefore instructed to re- ply to Mr. Arthur to that effect.
THE MILE " SLIDE " AT MOORE STATION.

A letter was read from Mr. W. D. Houghton calling atten- tion to a " slipe" erected at Moore station by which milk cans are let down from the bridge on to the platform, and stating that to get to the slide the footpath had to be crossed, that the cans were placed on a little plot of land at the top of the slide, and that damage was thereby caused to Mr. Houghton's hedge and wall. Mr. Houghton had written to the Railway Company, but the company's engineer had refused to protect the hedge and wall far fear of committing the company to any liability.—The CHAIRMAN: But any- body crossing the footpath is breaking the law.—The CLERK: That is a question, sir. How would you get to your house if you didn't cross the footpath ?—The CHAIRMAN said the land did not belong to the Board, so they could not take any action with respect to that; and as for the obetruc- tion on the footpath, that was a matter for the police.

MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL-

RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT RUNCORN. On Thursday evening a meeting of owners and rate- payers, convened by Dr. Steele, the chairman of the Com- mise!oners, was held in Bethesda schoolroom, for the pur- pose of obtaining their consent to an opposition in Parlia- ment by the Runcorn Board of Commissioners to the Man- chester Snip Canal Bill. Dr. Steele presided, and there were present Messrs. Robert Shaw, W. Handley, J. W. Lightburn, W. Fistier, J. R. Frith, Win. Whittaker, F. Fairhurst, T. liandley, J. Williams, F. A. Like, P. Speakman. W. H. Chadwick, W. H. Linaker, ym. Brookes. &e. —The CHAIR- -31•11 explained why the meeting was called, and Mr. W. Ifse.armsse asked if there was a copy of the bill there. He was answered in the negative,- but Mr. LINAKER said the scheme proposed would interfere with the town's drainage, with the approaches of the foreshore, and also with the scouring of the river. There was no special clause with re- gard to Runcorn —Mr. W. HANDLEY observed that they ought to see that the drainage was provided for, but he had seen no bill yet, and cattainly not of late years, where the drainage having been allowed to be cut off, provision was not made for carrying it out to the river. With regard to the scouring of the river there must be some mistake in the minds of the Commissioners. He had heard that Widnes and Warrington were opposing the bill be- cause the scouring was going to come to the Runcorn side. U that were so, it was quite clear that the Runcorn side of the river must be vastly hnproved, and Runcorn would be greatly benefited. He was at one with the Commissioners with regard to the absorption of the port. After the struggle that Runcorn had to obtain the port, he thought they ought not to lightly part with it. But he did not -know whether these rights would be better preserved by a friendly arrangement than by opposition, and he should be glad to propose a resolution to that effect, the cost of such an arrangement to be drawn from the rates. Mr. LINAKER said they must get in a position to oppose, and endeavour to make an arrabgetnent. If the :promoters would not give them what they wanted, the Board could insist upon their demands being satisfied.—Mr. LIGHTBURN observed tat the Com- mis.sioners had on a previous occasion approached the canal 4cheme in such a friendly manner that the promoters would listen to their representations with that fairness and con- sideration to which Mr. Handley had referred. But they were not therefore to leave themselves unprotected. They ough to place themselves in the best possible position by being a ale to oppose the scheme, and, secure their due rights.—Mr. SH.Aw remarked that it was not very long since they were told in that place that the canal would be of such advantage to Runcorn, and they were induced to put them- Selves out of the ordinary course, and ask for a certain thing to be done with reference to a Committee of the House of Commons. If they saw no difficulty then it was only right that the chairman should show why now they saw danger ahead. He stated without fear of contradiction that they stood in exactly the same position as they did then. There was nothing in the bill which affected the drainage ef Run- corn, for had they done it would not have been listened to. Then the promoters were not allowed to do anythinrs with the river from the point where they began to cut the land by the Old Quay docks; but they did take the water from Runcorn, ana it the portion of the scheme now before the Houses of Parliament was passed, they took way the facili- ties for carrying on the trade of Runcorn—(hear, hear)— because any of those present who had any experience of the river, knew that if they took away the "scour," in three months' time there would be no deep at Runcorn. By the scheme it was proposed to cot a channel in the centre of the river, and into this channel the scour would be sent, and in a short time they in Runcorn would have no access what- ever to the river, and even a flit would not be able to reach the docks. The owners of works in Runcorn had a greater stake than any ef the other ratepayers in reference to this scheme (hear, hear) and he considered the traders were making a great mistake in not combin- ing themselves together to oppose this bill con- jointly with the Commissioners, so that the expense might be lessened—The CHAIRMAN interposed, and said mrne of the traders had already forwarded a petition to Par- Lament.—Mr. Straw said one or two traders had, but as a whole they had not done N.—The CHAIRMAN: All the more reason why the ratepayers should.—Mr. SHAW went on to say that he was strongly in favour of opposing the bill, for the scheme if carried out would interfere with the present

their control will thus be most seriously injured and incon- venienced, and the present system of drainage in the town will be destroyed and your petitioners put to great expense and trouble in providing other means of drainage. The stopping up of and interference with the said streets and roads will also cause the greatest inconvenience to your petitioners and the inhabitants of their district, and seriously deprecate the value of property in the neighbour- hood of such streets. _ _ _

6. The works propcsed to be authorised in connection with the banks, beds, shores, and channels of the river's Mersey and Irwell, the construction of the new canal, the impounding of the water of the rivers Mersey and Irwell, and other waters mentioned in the , bill, and the diversion of such waters into the new ship canal will serieusly affect the river Mersey at and near Runcorn below the new canal. The Said waters will flow from the said ship canal into the river Mersey in entirely different channels,and in different quantities than at present, and your petitioners are advised and believe that the effect may be to form banks in the bed of the river Mersey and to ob- struct the access to thq Runcorn docks and prevent the further extension of decks at Runcorn, thereby causing great injury to the commercial prosperity of the town. Such silting up would also prevent the efficient discharge of the sewage of the whole town into the said river. 7. It is also proposed by the bill that the rivets Mersey and Irwell, from Eastham Ferry, near Garston to Hunt's Bank in Manchester and the new canal, and all channels, canals, docks, and works of the company within those limits, are to be constituted the harbour and port of Man- chester' and. the company are to be the harbour authority thereof. _ .

8. The town of Runcorn is situated within those limits, and the harbour and docks of that place, which are now ex- tensively used by the inhabitants and traders of your peti- tioners' district, will become subject to the control and di- rection.of the new company as the harbour authority, and the commercial interests of the town of Runcorn will thus, to a great extent, be placed in the hands of that company, whc may, and probably will, endeavour to divert to Man- chester and the new ship canal, all trade now using Runcorn as its port, which port embraces a large portion of the river Mersey from Warrington to Dungeon Point and Lice, and has certain rights and privileges appertaining thereto; and for that purpose place obstacles in the way of the present , trade of Runcorn. _ _ _

9. The powers contained in the bill for the new company to purchase the undertaking of the Duke of Bridgewater's canal will also enable the new c llnpany. by arrangement with the present owners of the Duke of Bridgewater's navi- gation (who it is feared may not be adverse thereto) to par- chase and place under their own control the Bridgewater canal from Runcorn to Manchester, which now forms one of the water communications available for traffic be- tween those towns, and is of great advantage to the town of Runcorn, and rour petitioners submit that if your Honourable House should see fit to authorise the new ship canal the new company should not, in the interests of the towns of Runcorn and other places now accommodated by the said Bridgewater Canal, be allowed to purchase that under- taking, but that the same should remain an alternative and coupling route from Manchester to the estuary of the river Mersey. The new ship.canal would not be available for much of the traffic which now makes use of the said Bridgewater Canal by reason of that canal being intended for a different class of traffic from the ordinary inland barge and lighter traffic, and the , tolls chargeable thereon being fixed at rates which would be entirely prohibitory for such last-mentioned traffic. 10. The construction of the proposed ship canal and the other proposals of the bill are unnecessary and uncalled for by any public requirements. Your peti: )ners therefore humbly pray that the bill may not be allowcd to pass into law as it now stands, and that they may be heard by their counsel, agents, and witnesses against the preamble of the bill, and the clauses and provi- sions thereof, and may have such other relief in the premises as to your honourable House may seem meet. And your petitioners will ever pray. •

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, APRIL 7, 1883 A TRIBUTE FROM WARRINGTON LIBERALS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, APRIL 7, 1883 A TRIBUTE FROM WARRINGTON LIBERALS.
WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION

Tha interest taken in this contest is of the most feeble kind, and may be said to be wholly reflected from the walls by means of three placards. The first of these calls upon the ratepayers to support the nominees of the associations on the ground that they will best preserve the rights of the community, while the second, signed "A workingman and a , Good Templar," contains an attack upon Mr. Hargreaves--or at least upon his occupation as a publican. The ratepayers are asked not to vote for a man who "lives on the souls" of his fellow creatures and "sent up the poor rate." To-day will show whether they complied with the request, Dr. O'Keeffe, who is one of the association's midi._ dates, has issued a manifesto in which he expresses his dis- approval of the compact entered into by the rival rate- payers' organization to deprieve the electors of their rights of citizenship. He contends that if they hid really wished to save the expense of a contest, instead of wishing Mr. Hargreaves to suit the fight, one of their nominees would have resigned. Dr. O'Keeffe here points out a course,which he apparently dees not see fit to follow himself, and we most regard it as another example of preaching without precept. However, the election he decided. The papers were collected yesterday, and will be counted to-day. The result will probably be made known daring the evening.

PRESENTATION TO MR. H. ROBERTS. April 2nd, 1883, the third anniversary of the election of a Liberal Parliamentary representative for the borough of 1 Warrington, was chosen by the members of the party of 1 progress in the town as a fitting occasion on which to pre- sent Mr. Henry Roberts, the Liberal agent, with a token of their appreciation of his services during the last decade. It is a very short time since the movement was originated, but the ready response to the private appeal for subscriptions abundantly testified the high estimate the Liberals of War- rington have of Mr.Roberts's zealous services to his party. Their tribute to Mr. Roberts is of a most substantial and serviceable character, comprising a handsome Brinsmead piano, a walnut secretaire (by Garnett and Sons), a gold watch and guard (by Zimmerman), and a beautiful album, containing an address and the names of the subscribers. The presentation took place on Monday evening, in the committee-room at the Liberal Club, and the very room besides the nature of the gathering brought to the minds of many the pleasant scenes which occurred there that day three years ago. The pro- ceedings commenced with a knife and fork tea, to which about 40 persons sat down, the caterer being Mr. C. Cassidy, the new manager. Mr. Councillor Monks was called to the chair after tea, and he was supported by Mr. H. Roberts, Mr. J. H. Gornall, Mr. S. Barlow, and the Rev. J. fonge ; and there were also present Messrs. T. Morris (vice-chairman), Thomas Jones, John Bonnell, Richard Roberts, G. Plumpton, Jos. Ailinsen, J. W. Hall, M. Knowles, E. Place, Jos. Mounfield, jour., Jas. Strange, J. Garner, T. S. Fairclough, W. Bibby, Jas. Taylor, G. Clay, R. Greenwood, W. Jefferys, Jos. Knowles, G. Wallington, junr., J. Donoghue, W. Burrows, J. Mullins, W. Croskill, L. Gillooley, W. Roberts, S. Ounbobbin, W. Unsworth, W. Dyson, R. Campbell, F. Murray, and U. Cassidy. Mr. S. Ban Low read the following letters : Westminster Palace Hotel, 31st March.—My dear 81r,I regret greatly that I am not able to be with you at the pre- sentation to Mr. Roberts. I have been confined to my rooms for three weeks by an attack of bronchitis, and I am still "sick and in prison," I need no say how much the feelings which have prompted this gift to Mr. Roberts have my entire sympathy. I know as well as any one the services be has rendered to his party, and I am sure that this acknowledge- ment has been richly merited by earnest and zealous and successful efforts on his pert during the lrst ten yew s. The _,,mplirnent must be gratifying to Mr. Roberts, and the manner in which the movement has been catried out by those who had be‘n active in it is honourable to them and to him. —I am, dear sir, yours faithfully, J. G. MCMINNIES.—Mr. S. Barlow. The }lollies, Latchford, Warrington.—Dear Mr. Barlow,—l really cannot tell you how sorry I shall be not to be with you all at the presentation of the testimonial to •,Mr. Hy Roberts It has been a great plea-ure to me to join in' this testimonial. and I should have considered it not only a pleasure but an honour to have occupied the important position you had de- signed for me on the occasion. 1 have a great respect for Kr. Roberts, and a great admiration for his untiring devotion to our party Ability may be bought, but such untiring devotion as that of Mr Roberts is beyond price. What I admire so much is Mr Roberts' persistency. His attention to, and his Interest in. whatever concerns the psrty, never fails and never flags Be is always there when wanted. We cannot over- estiniaa e what this quality has done for the party, and how much our present satisfactory position is owing to Mr. Roberts's waachiul zeal. I can truly say that my heart will be wi,h you on Monday evening, and that my enforced absence is a real disappointment. Please express this to the meeting.— Yours very truly, CHARLES BROADBENT. Armitage and Rigby's, Oockhedge Mills, Warrington, 2nd April, IBB3.—My dear am sorry to be unable to attend the presentation to Mr. Henry Roberts this evening, as in ommoa with all members of the Liberal Association lam quite aware how much we owe to him for his indefatigable exertions in connection with our w rk in the borough. Hoping that you may have a pleasant evening. —I am, yours very truly, ZIBA ARMITAGE. The toast of "The Queen," having been drunk, The CHAIRMAN gave the " Liberal party." He thought there could be no question that to the Liberal party of this country a great deal of the prosperity and a great deal of the stability of the country was owing. Not that he under- rated the value of an opposition when rightly conducted, but he thought Mr. Chamberlain was quite right in saying the other night that at the present time the Tory party was rather a party of obstruction than of opposition. (Hear, hear.) He thought the time was coming when a stop would be put to this obstruction, and when the work of the Liberal party would be proceeded with in a satisfactory manner. (Hear, hear.) If there was an everlasting obstruction no progress was possible, and be hoped the present session would see the last of obstruction. As the local Liberal party they were directly interested in the return of Mr. McMinnies to Parliament, but it would require all their efforts to maintain the supremacy which they had attained. Some of the leaders of the Tory party were indulging in the hope that at the next election, they may be able to reverse the state of affairs. The ether day he happened to meet one of them ia a railway carriage, and he spoke rather sanguinely of the result of the next election; but he ven- tured to intimate that there was not the shadow of a chance, because the Liberal party were more united now than even at the last election. (Hear, hear.) While the Tories seemed to make a goad deal of the Irish difficulty, he himself did not anticipate any difficulty in the way of uniting with themselves the Irish and Catholic Liberals in the town. ( Applause.) He proposed with hearty goodwill the toast of "Liberal party of this country, and the Liberal party of Warrington in particular." (Applause.) The Rev. J. YONGE responded. He remarked that he thought they might congratulate themselves on the condi- tion of the Liberal party in the country. The very fact that their friends the enemy were all of them sixes and sevens in their endeavour to establish anything like a reasonable op- position, he thought was a decided testimony of the strength of the Liberal party in the kingdom at the present time. (Hear, hear.) In regard to the Liberal party in the borough he thonght they might congratulate themselves upon its very substantial, united, and compact condition, but he re- mieded them that it would be a sad thing for them as a party if they presumed upon past success, and at all relaxed their endeavours to keep Liberalism in the upper hand in the town of Warrington. He had a strong conviction, as he was sure every gentleman in the room had, that the present position of the Liberal party in War- rington was very largely owing to the honest and earnest endeavours of their friend whom they were met to honour that evening. He thought they must all feel that the testimonial was a reasonable tribute to one who had de- voted his intelligence and activity and earnestness to the cause which they had so much at heart. (Applause). They could say, with honesty to their friend, Mr. Roberts had worked well for the party, and they looked to him for sub- stantial service in days and years to come. (Applause). Mr. T. S. FAIRCLOIIGH also responded, and said though he should not advise the Liberal party to be anything but care- ful in their movements, be thought they had nothing to fear so long as they bad such is man as Mr. Gladstone at their head, and the other party such a hybrid sort of Churchill- Salisbury-Cross. (Loud laughter.) Mr. S. Bertrow gave" our esteemed member." A more consistent politician no town or borough •in England pro- duced than Mr. McMinnies, who on every occasion tbey found a perfect gentleman and a thoroaghly sociable friend. (Applause.) The toast was drunk with great enthusiasm.

Mr. J. IL GOtNALL then rose amid applause, and said:' Mr..Cbairman and fellow Liberals, I rise with feelings of great pleasure to fulfil the duty the committee have ac- corded to me of formally presenting to Mr. Henry Roberts an address expressing our admiration for his character as a man, and our gratitude to him for steering the Liberal cause to a sure,. and I hope, a lasting victory in this berough. (Applause.) In this album is recorded the fact that such was the value we placed on his laleours that we ask him to graciously accept as a memento of his valuable services, a piano, a seeretaire, and a watch, all of the best quality. (Heir, bear.) Ten years ago the position of the Liberal party in this borough was in a critical condition, and we suffered a defeat in 1874. On the 12th February, 1873, Mr. Roberts was _appointed agent to the party. In a very short time after the defeat, such was the tact and ability which Mr. Roberts exerted in forwarding the interests of the political party to which we are so proud to belong, that at the annual revisions there were signs that our de- feat was only of a temporary character. There was a con- stant accession to our milli's, though it is a matter of history that he other side invariably published statements to the effect that Toryism still dominated in this town. (Hear, hear.) I well recollect that a few' evenings before the memorable victory we commemorate to-day, after a general review of our position Mr. McMinnies said that "the result of the election would not be a mere defeat, but a complete route of the enemy "—(applause)—and the majority of 529 proved that we knew- in whom we believed. (Loud applause.) Though we have one of the grandest men in Lancashire to represent us—(applause—and leaders of whom any consti- tuency may feet proud—(hear, hear)—l know they will agree with me when I say that the success on the 2nd April, MO, was in no small degree due to the unvarying diligence and assiduous attention to his duties of our Liberal agent. Applause) lam well aware that there are some people who would say it is the duty of all who are paid for their labours to discharge them in a faithful manner. Granted; but Mr. Roberts has done more than this. (Hear. hear.) And why ? Because his heart is in the right place.—(hear, hear)—be sympathises with every political aspiration that is to pro- mote the h-mpiness of the thousands in one room ; . and Liberelism wi:l be untrue to its grearprinciplea if it fails to endeavour to remove every vistage of injustice which presses on the great mass of the people. (Applause.) :Mr. Bright said the other day that he bad a great regard for the Chinese, because they supplied us with the cup that cheered but did not inebriate. Well, we have been enjoying that whelesome stimulant, and I will tell you that from a most intimate knowledge of Mr. Roberts, a great measure of his success is due to. the fact that he was bred and born:a believer in the principles of temperance. (Applause.) Another element of his success has been the courteous and strightforward manner in which he has treated friend and foe. (Hear, hear.) I believe the Tories even like him, and only wish they had an agent equal to him. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Under his guidance every phase and class of Liberalism is recognised in our association. Catholic and Protestant, employer and employed, English- men, Irishmen, Scotchmen, and Welshmen, are all fellow- werkers in pr:.•.moting the Liberal faith. I believe also that his deep sympathy with tho cause of Irelaod has been of great service in stimulating our efforts. (Applause.) There is still week for Liberals to do; as my friend, Mr. Lloyd Jones, said th e other day,we have only just began. (Applause.) We owe much yet to Ireland. The English landlords will

have to be dealt with, the franchise must be extended, the PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Bonnell, Mr. J. Mullins (as a fidgeted in their seats and looked " unutterable things."— Catholic), Mr. G. Wallington, Mr. J. Albinson, Mr. J. W. After a pause, Mr. TVRER suggested that the better plan Hall (as a temperance politician), Mr. L. Gillooley (as an would be for the clerk to ask for a general authority to deal Irishman), Mr. Dyson, and the Chairman also spoke in most with such cases rather than a special authority to deal with complimentary terms of Mr. Roberts's conduct and services, the particular case, and it was agreed that Mr. Hartley should do so Mr. H. ROBERTS, who was received with loud applause on rising to reply, said: I can assure you it is with consider- able difficulty I rise to say the few words that I shall say on the present occasion. lam painfully conscious that a ' great deal too much has been made to-night of the services which I have endeavoured to render the greats Liberal ' cause in Warrington, and I should be very sorry indeed if anything which has been said of myself should in any way depreciate the assistance which I have received—the voluntary assistance which I have received—from so many of the prominent members of the Liberal party in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) It is quite true that I have been in your. service for 10 years, and it is quite true the Liberal party in Warrington is to-day in a considerably better position than it was 10 years ago; but you must not forget that a very small portion of the success in that re- spect is attributable to myself. If ,I had not had my hands supportdd by men like our worthy chairman and the esteemed member for the borough he one way, and my work carried out in honest detail by the ward secretaries,' and the members of the ward committees, it would have been utterly impossible for me to have done anything like what has been referred to to-night. (Hear, hear.) I have had all kinds of Viings to pass throngh- during the 10 years—times of dissappointment, times of trial, times of success; and I have never yet re- ceived anything but sympathy in either the one or the other. (Hear, hear.) When we have been defeated we have mourned together, and we have sympathised together. When we have been successful we have rejoiced together; and I don't remember a single occasion on which any man has pointed a finger to me in time of defeat, or has intimated in any way that he attributed that defeat to any want of energy or goodwill in regard to myself. (Hear, hear.) If you consider yourselves fortunate—if I may use the words —in having me as your secretary, I consider myself equally or more fortunate in having bad such a Liberal party as I Ind in Warrington as my masters. (Hear, hear.) Reference has been made to the fact that one does not work altogether for the pay that one receives in reference to matters of this kind. I can assure you honestly that no political agent,—whether Liberal or Conservative—who does his duty honestly to his party can be repaid by the salary which he receives. (Hear' hear.) Unless he believes thoroughly in the prin- ciples his party advocates, and believes those principles to be necessary for the happiness and welfare of the country, and that they deserve his sympathy and strenous efforts for their success, 1 say he is utterly unworthy of the position which he aspires to in reference to that matter. Now, sir, at the present moment we are ourselves happily situated in War- rington; but Ido not think the Tory party is anything like so disorganised or disunited as to make us feel so safe that we can look apathetically to the future: I ventured to say the day after the election, just three years ago, while we had passed through a severe fight, in which all or nearly in this room were engaged, the next fight will be more severe, more difficult than that one had been; and I may say that I still believe the Conservative party in Warring- ton will make a yet more determined fight in which all the forces which are at their command will be brought to play, to wrest, if possible, the seat from the Liberal party. There is only one thing needed in order to make that ntterly im- possible. If, as has been so frequently done by the Liberals, of Warrington, we are content to sink for a moment any 'matters of a mere personal character, if we are content not to let matters of detail disturb us, if we are content to go in for the good of the party itself—united as strongly as we shall be, it will be utterly impossible for the Tory party to do anything in that direction. I shall net be satisfied, if my health is spared, to take away my hand from the work of the Liberal party in Warrington as its agent until I believe our position to be thoroughly impregnable. Of course, looking forward to the future, I cannot say what circumstance may arise which may make it difficult, more or less, for me to retain that position ; but at the present time I see no reason why,e if you continue to retain confidence in me, I should not in the future, as in the past, render you my services with the hope and strong desire that the day will soon come when Toryism in Warrington will be a defeated thing. (Applause.) I cannot find words in which to express to Dr. Gornall and the gentlemen who have spoken, the feelings which I have to- wards them for their great kindness to-day. be testimonial which you have presented to me is in itself both handsome and costly. As long as I live I shall look upon these things which you have given to me with the greatest pride and satisfaction. lam very grateful to you for the kind manner in which you received the name of my wife, and when I tell you that she is as good a Liberal as I am—(applause)— and that she has in her own way done everything which it is possible for a woman to do, to aid the success of the party in Warrington, I am sure that you will, as you have done, think of her with the same kindness and respect as you have done myself. I trope my children will look upon these things, and think as they grow older, that after all it is worth something to be a Liberal. I an a Liberal from principle and conviction. I belong to a body of denominationalists who owe to the Liberal party every privilege that they possess; and when I look back and read the history of my church, and remember the petty persecutions that they received at the hands of the Tory party, I am puzzled beyend measure to understand how any Dissenter can be anything but a strong Liberal. (Hear, hear.) do not care what denomination a man belongs to, if he has within him a spirit of fair play, if he has a desire that all purely class distinctions shall be re- moved, and all men stand equal before the law, that man cannot be anything but a Liberal, because those are the very principles which lie at the foundation of Liberalism in this country. (Applause.) lam very proud to think what little I have done in reference to the Irish and Catholic party in Warrington has been appreciated. What I have done has only been from a sense of this : that it would be most unfair—l cannot conceive how any man of broad views can think otherwise than that it would be most unfair—and improper that, for any differences in religious opinion, there should- be any political difference between Protestants and Catholics; and so long as lam connected with the Liberal party, either officially or unofficially, so long shall I make it my en- deavour to do everything I can to promote a feeling of goodwill between the various sections of the party. (Ap- plause.) In all my efforts in this direction 1 hare been most kindly and warmly received by the Catholic clergy Of this town. (Applause.) I know there are some people who seem to think that there is something about Catholic clergymen that is not altogether as they wish. Let me say this, that from what I have seen of the Catholic clergy of this town—and I have been very intimately in connection with them—l never met a body of men who seemed to me to possess more thoroughly and .truly the spirit of our Saviour than the Catholic clergy do. (Applause.) Well, sir, I won't take up your time longer. This is not an occasion on which I feel perfectly free, or I would speak at greater length. But I hope in the future this beautiful instrument which you have given me will be often used and sweet sounds discoursed from it in celebration of greater Liberal victories; I hope when I am doing work at that handsome seeretaire I may be able to plan fresh projects with which to defeat the enemy I trust when T look at the album I shall be reminded by the names there written, of the faces of dear friends whom I es- teem, and who esteem me; and when I look at the watch I hope I shall be reminded that time is precious,-and be able to take a better ideal of my duty to my God, and my duty to any fellow-man. ( Loud applause.) The healths of the chairman and vice-chairman were then drunk; and

THE LUNCHEON QUESTION AGAIN. - A WARVI DISCUSSION.

The CLERK read the following letter from Mr. J. 0. Swift,i solicitor, St. Helens:—"Re Deneett. You will no doubt ' have received notice of counter claim herein, and I suppose it will come before the Guardians at their ordinary meeting. I really hope they will new see their way to settle Mr. Dennett's claim, considering the smallness of the sum in question and the suggestion that has been made by the Guaraians themselves for raising the money to settle it. I think if you would bring the matter before them again they would see their way to pay the claim. . Please do what you can."—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said he should very much like to see the bill paid. He had offered a sovereign towards it before, and he would be quite willing to repeat that offer whether he had the privilege of sitting at that Board again or not It was a disgrace to the Guardians.—Mr. HALL: That is very strong language. I was not present, and never had a dinner connected witb the matter, and am I to be included in the disgrace ?—Rev. T. CHAMBERS: I was not, here either, but it is a disgrace to.the Board as it then existed.— Mr. GERRARD: The money was paid by the Boani. It was the Master who did not pay it over to Mr. Dennett.—Mr. HALL: He has fought it with the Local Government Board,. and in the County Court and failed, and yet it is cropping up continually.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS: That is the reason I say the money should be paid.—Mr. HALL: I should like to explain this matter. Mr. Dennett, when his account was sent in every quarter, allowed a certain deduc- tion to be made. Why did he allow it? Because he knew there was an arrangement between himself and the governor of the house that at the end of the yeat he would be paid the amount of money deducted from his account. If he was dissatisfied, why -did he not return his cheque? He sent in a bill for £5OO, and allowed so much to be taken off. Mr. Archer collected the money for each dinner during the whole period, and at the end of the year there was a deficiency which the Guardians paid. Mr. Archer left the Workhouse, and unfortunately the money went with him. Then Mr. Dennett raised the question why the money was not paid. He should have raised the ques- tion when his account was docked. When Mr. Dennett got the Indian corn he did it with a view of securing the other account. But it is not good enough. We paid for the Indian corn and we want payment back agiin.—Mr. NEW- SOME: Is the explanation that the Guardians paid for this to the late master and that-he never paid Mr. Dennett ? Mr. HALL: Yes.—Mr. NEWSOME : Then I don't think the Guardians should pay it again.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS: I am still of opinion that whatever discrepat.cy there may have been between the butcher and the master, it would add to the dignity of this Board if we paid the man's bill.—The subject dropped.
