div.head: DRAMATIC PERFORAIATSCE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: DRAMATIC PERFORAIATSCE AT RUNCORN.

The amateur dramatists connected with St. Edward's Catholic schools gave a performance in Runcorn Public Hall on Tuesday evening, in aid of the funds of that religions institution. There was a large audience. The pro- gramme commenced with a short musical entertainment, in which the Irish National Foresters band. Miss Jameson, and Miss Hewitt took part. "Fading away" was sung by Miss Jameson with much pathos and power, her voice being clear and of good compass. Miss Hewitt gave a capital renderineof the song "Shells of the ocean," and she was loudly applauded. Then followed the comic drama Pike O'Calligan." The stige accessories to the piece were very suitable, and the performance as a whole"was excellent. As Pike O'Calligan, a faithful adherent to Neil O'Connor, an attainted rebel,. Mr. T. Williamson displayed much ability and a high sense of humour, his impersonation being a most admirable one. Mr. J. Williamson, who took the role of Neil O'Connor, lacked the dignity necessary to the full realisation of the character, but his acting otherwise was not without some good points. In Mr. J. Coleman, Sir James Blackadder, a royalist, had a worthy exponent, an indistinctness of utterance, which may be easily overcome, marring, however, to some extent, the effect. Rarely have we seen amateur lady dramatists act better than Miss Parker and Mrs. Mutch, in the respective characters of Honor O'Calligan, wife of Pike, and Lady Broughton, betrothed to Neil. Miss Parker's pourtrayal of the hot tempered Irish peasant's wife was deserving of all praise and the hearty laughter of the audience was a sufficient indication of their appreciation. Mrs. Mutch's impersonation was dis- tinguished by dimity and power of expression, especially noticeable in the scene when she spurns Sir James, and beards him in his own domain. Mr. J. Parker was a capital Red Rufus, the spy and in- former, the other characters being Sergeant Snipes, a man of discipline, Mr. H. Rooney; James, a servant, Mr. R. Williamson ; Captain Wilson, Mr. T. Reilly; Patrick and Jemmy, Pike's children, Masters Williamson and Coleman. In the interval the band played a selection, and Messrs. Mulvaney and Stoner gave a song and dance entitled "Ire- land and America," which appeared to be much enjoyed. The duet "Mother, can this glory be," was sung by Miss Jameson and Miss Hewitt, with unimpeachable taste, their voices blending harmoniously. The performance concluded with the farce "The Irish doctor," which provoked much merriment. Mr. Mulvaney, in the two-fold character of Dennis Murphy, a broom maker, and Dr. Murphy, a professor of medicine, acted with fitting humour, and roars of laughter greeted his eccentricities; while Mr. Stoner, as Bridget, wife of Dennis, showed equal ability. The other characters which were well sustained were :—Sir Ralph Credulous, Mr Coleman; Walter Love- well, Mr J. Williamson; Squire Robert, Mr J. Parker; Laura Credulous, Mrs Mutch ; Peggy, her maid, Miss Parker; Doctor Frantic, Mr Coleman; and Simon, Dick, and Robin, servants, Mr Williamson.

div.head: MR. lIP'_NRY WOODS AND MR. LUKE FILDES.
div.p: MR. lIP'_NRY WOODS AND MR. LUKE FILDES.

The Daily Telegraph, in an article on the studios, says : " Mr.H.Woods has a Venetian picture. 'Preparing for the First Communion,' in which some women,who have been preparing a veil, are showing it on a child for the critical judgment of 1 the priest. The scene is in the open air, and the surround- ings are all very characteristic. 'The Village Wedding.' intended by Mr. Luke Fildes, A.R.A., for the Royal Academy, is a realistic representation of a nuptial party coming down a rustic street from the church." The Daily News says :—" Mr. Henry Woods, A.R.A., whose last sea- son pictures of open-air Venetian life are fresh in the re- collection, will this year be content to send in one picture to the Academy. Preparing for the First Communion' 1 among Venetian fisher-folk has in it many amusing as well as interesting aspects. The little girl who is to be the com- municant stands modestly wearing the veil on the pavement outside of her father's house answering the questions of a robust-looking priest. The father of the girl is seated on a stool and looks on with a critical air while he fills his pipe; but he is not the only person intetested. His wife and his mother, his smaller children, and a couple of girls who are making the degenerate modern successor of point de Venise, are all heart and soul in the proceedings. Mr. Luke Fildes, A.R A., has this year put forth his strength in a large gal- lers‘picture entitled 'A Village Wedding, and treated with strict adherence to realism. The happy pair head the pro- cession returning from the church seen at the other end of the village street. Faces and clothes are alike of rustic outlin,s, dignity being given to the group by the addition of Lifeguardsman with a distinctly military cast of features. As the wedding party goes by it is accompanied and viewed with various feelings by the spectators. There is one enthu- siastic little girl running in front like a rustic harbingeir and a boy with a basketful of provisions which, carried away by the excitement of the wedding, he is neglecting to deliver. In the main the lookers-on are sympathe lc, but there is a critical, or rather inquiring air about a tall, red-haired damsel, and one sturdy dame is standing at - her door with arms akimbo, net advancing a yard to wish the young couple God speed.' There is an immense number of figures in this picture, all excepting the Lifeguardsm in of the rustic type." A London correspondent writes "It is not possible to say as yet what will be the character of the Royal Academy Exhibition to ba opened next month. save only that it will bt particularly strong in portraits. I notice that Mr. Ottless is himself sanding six. There will be general regret that Mr. Holman Hunt has not been able to complete in time his reproduction of the • Flight into Egypt,' the original of which had been abandoned on account of the cockling 'of the canvas. It will probably he ready for exhibition later in the season. Warrington folk who remember Mr. Luke Files will have a keen I interest in his wedding,' which was expected last year, and is now so perfect as to promise to be one of the best things in the exhibition."

div.head: WARRINGTON BUILDER'S PETITION.
div.p: A WARRINGTON BUILDER'S PETITION.

In the Lancashire Court of Chancery, on Thursday, be- fore Vice-Chancellor Bristowe, and in the matter of the International Marine Hydropathic Company, Limited, Mr. Thatch applied for an order of the Court directing a compul- sory minding up. The Company carried on their business at Seaforth, near Liverpool, and the petition is that of a creditor, Mr. R. W. Collin, builder' Warrington. The Company opened, a short time ago, a hydropathic bathing establishment at Seaforth, and the petitioner stated that they owed him a stain of £5,021 for work done and material supplied, and that other creditors for considerable amounts would be able, in a few days, to enforce judgment. Since the establishment was opened the Company had carried on businees at a large and serious loss, and the petition stated that the C y ompan was wholly unable to pay its debts, and ought, therefore, -to be compulsory wound up.—Mr. Retch stated that a Mr. Stead, of Liverpoel, who had been ap- pointed provisional liquidator, bad !nada an affidavit in which he stated that there were three creditors' actions pending, and that an order had been /made for the payment of a large amount of rates which were due. and that in addition a sum of £20,000 was this to unsecured creditors. Mortgages to the extent of £33500 bad been called in and six months in- terest was owing to one of them for £25,000, which had not been paid because there was no money available for the pur- pose. Having made a careful estimate of the assets Mr. Stead was of opinion that they would not realise more than £5OOO. A meeting was held at the Company's preniises at Seaforth on March 30, at which the Directors present stated that the Company was unable to carry out the terms of an arrangement with the creditors which had been entered into, baYing no funds with which to pay the debts. Mr. Ne- ville who app.iared for the Company, asked that further ti'me%hould be allowed. The Directors were, he stated. try- ing to raise a sum of £50,000 for the purpose of paying off the first mortgage and 10s. in the pound to the creditors. It would be a pity, if by that arrangement, the winding-up could be prevented, that the order applied for should now be made.—The Vice-Chancellor said he thought the Com- pany ought to be wound up compulsorily, and made the usual winding-up order, authorising the provisional liquida- tor to carry on the businesa till the appointment of an official liqeidator-under certain conditions.

SERVICE OF SONG AT RUNCORN. -On Thursday evening a service of song, entitled "The Saviour King," was given in Shaw-street school-room to a good audience. The choir was composed of members from the Parish Church, Newtown Mission, and St. Paul's, Bethesda, Primi- tive Methodist, and Ellesmere-street Chapels; and numbered 60 voices. Under the conductorship of MY. C. Pownall they acquitted themselves with great credit, and the soloists, Me. C. Porinall and Miss Horton, each sang with good effect. The Rev. J. J. Bryant read the narrative, and Mr. Johnson wedded at the harmonium.

div.head: NEW FINANCIAL YEAR.
div.p: THE NEW FINANCIAL YEAR.

The CLERK, in submitting the contribution orders for the ensuing half-year, remarked that it would be gratifying both to the Guardians and the public to know that they were considerably less than they had been for some time. Last year they called for £4,000 more than they waited for county rate purposes, basing the estimate upon what they bad paid in preceding half-years. They had given the townships credit for that differenCe, and they had recovered from Government nearly £2,000 in the shape of lunacy ex- penses, salaries of medical officers, and druga for the wash- house, and had given credit for thi3se items also, so that in- stead of having, as in the previous year, to make a call for £26,478, they were this time only asking for £18.782, and they were trusting that they would not have anything of an usual character in the next six months to contend with. I They had a balance owing from Ditton of £169, and from I Widnes of £2,000. The contribution orders, which were made in three instalments payable 17th April, 15th May, and 12th June, were as follows :—Much Woolton £375, Little WoolCon£279, Windte £142, Widnes £7;128. L EWI:S'S IN LIVERPOOL, AND THE PROVIDING OF THE BEST TEA TO FAMILIES, HOTELS, AND PUBLIC AND PRIVATE INSTITUTIONS THROUGH- OUT TUE UNITED KINGDOM. Who are Lewis's? Well, lewcs's are as well known in Liver- pool as the Bank of England is known is London. Lewis's began business in Liverpool thirty years ago, and Lewis's have at this present time one of the very largest businesses n Eng- land. Lewis's have not always sold Tea, but having a very large number of employes to provide with an afternoon meal, Lewis's were struck with the difficulty of procuting a gotd drinkable and refreshing Tea for them at a moderate price. The ordinary Teas were perfectly tab •minable. Tired of the constant andnot unreasonable complaints and of the perpetual changing of their Tea Dealers, Lewis's at , last resolved to buy their Tea for the use of their establishment direct from tho shippers, and to en- gage a qualified person to make the purchase. ' Lewis's could hardly believe there .pould be such 4 change for the better in the cost and quality f.f the tea so bought, but "experience teaches." Lewis's th, vht what was good enough.for the use of all their establi,hments, public and private, would surely be good enough for the general public. Lewis's then began to sell Teas to their friend?, and at last were induced to make thesale public in Lancashire, where they sell 20,000 pounds of Tea per week. Lewis's now feel they have benefited only a small pro- portion of the population; they intend in future to snake their Tea known all over the United Kingdom. Lewis's pure, splendid Tea, is one stated price, 2s a pound. Lewis s have no other price Tea, neither higher nor lower, and this Two Shilling Tea is fit for the Queen to drink. Two shil- lings is a favourite pries with Lewis's, they having been able to supply the public with many excellent things at the price. Not tilt after much hard work did Lewis's succeed in blending a splendid and most deliciously-flavoured Tea, which they are giving to the public for 2s a pound. Many tea dealers charge the public 3s and 3s 64 for a simir quality. Lewis's desire to be the universal suppliers of Tea. Tea is drunk in every house- hold in the United Kingdom; it should therefore be sold at a less profit than any other article of consumption, except bread. Lewis's wish particularly to direct the attention of every family and every househo:der to the great advantage there is in buying Lewis's Twakihilling Tea. The flavour is so good and the strength so very great, that one p..und goes further than 18 ounces of most other Teas, providing always the water boils thoroughly. The proof that Lewis's do not exaggerate the appreciation in which their Two Shilling Tea is held lies in the fact that they receive thousands of orders every day from all parts of the United Kingdom. Lewis's would like members of the Press all over the United Kingdom to write for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tea; they are sure to be satisfied ard astonished with the result. Every hotel-keener, and every public and private institution throughout the country, should write to Lewis's in Liverpool for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tea. The risk is not great; it is only to send 2s in stamps to Lewis's in Liverpool, and in return they will receive a sound of splendid Tea, packed neatly in a hex. carriage paid. to any address in the United Kingdom. —Address Lewis's in Liverpool.
